app_description: Hi, I'm building a mental-health chatbot called SerenityBot. It uses an LLM (we fine-tuned Mistral-7B) to deliver CBT exercises for users with mild-to-moderate anxiety. Users chat with it daily, log their mood, and the bot adapts its responses based on past sessions. We're targeting young adults (18-30) in France and Switzerland. There's a crisis-keyword detector that pops up a hotline number.
developer_persona: Junior product manager at a 12-person startup, technically curious but light on regulation knowledge. Defensive when scope creep into 'medical device' territory is suggested.

simulated_answers.data_collected: We store chat transcripts, mood scores, session timestamps, and anonymized usage metrics. We don't ask for name or address, just email for login.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: There's a checkbox at signup saying 'I agree to the terms'. The privacy policy is a 14-page PDF.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: We're calling it a wellness app to avoid medical device classification. Our legal counsel said as long as we put 'not a substitute for therapy' in the disclaimer, we're fine.
simulated_answers.user_research: We did 8 interviews with potential users during design. No clinical psychologist on the team yet, but our CEO is talking to one.
simulated_answers.accessibility: We support French and English. We haven't tested with screen readers or users with cognitive impairments.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: We A/B tested the crisis-keyword detector against a held-out set of 200 messages flagged manually. F1 was 0.74.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: The LLM is Mistral-7B fine-tuned on ~10k CBT-style dialogues we generated synthetically using GPT-4. We do post-hoc moderation with a smaller classifier.
simulated_answers.post_market: We have crash analytics via Sentry. No clinical incident reporting workflow.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: We share aggregated usage stats with our investor. Chat content stays internal.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Users can delete their account from settings, which deletes all their data after 30 days.

expected_risks.risk: Almost certainly a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) under MDR — the disclaimer doesn't change the intended purpose. CBT delivery to users with anxiety is a medical intent.
Likely high-risk under EU AI Act (Annex III §1 health), requires conformity assessment, post-market monitoring, transparency.
No clinical validation of the CBT exercises or the chatbot's adherence to evidence-based protocols.
Consent is a single checkbox over a 14-page PDF — not informed consent for processing sensitive health data under GDPR Art. 9.
Young adults can include 18-year-olds with maturing autonomy; chat transcripts are special-category data.
Users with anxiety may use the bot as a substitute for professional care; no escalation to a clinician.
Daily engagement loop + mood logging may cultivate dependency or emotional reliance on the bot.
Disclaimer is buried; users may not understand the bot is not a therapist.
CBT exercises generated by an LLM may not be distinguishable from validated clinical content.
French/English only — Switzerland has German + Italian speakers; no cultural validation of CBT prompts.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Engage a Notified Body, classify as Class IIa SaMD under MDR Rule 11, prepare a technical file.
Map system to EU AI Act high-risk obligations: risk-management system, data governance docs, human oversight, transparency to users.
Run a single-arm pilot study with 50-100 users + standardized anxiety scale (GAD-7) pre/post, with a clinician on the team.
Layered consent UI: short summary + 'tell me more' expansions; separate consent for crisis-keyword detection and research use.
Mandatory weekly self-assessment; if GAD-7 ≥ 10 for 2 consecutive weeks, surface a 'please consider seeing a professional' nudge.
Visibly tag content as 'AI-generated CBT guidance' vs 'clinically reviewed' modules.

notes: Highest-stakes scenario: developer assumes 'disclaimer = not a medical device' (false). Must catch SaMD classification, EU AI Act, and lack of clinical validation. Crisis path is necessary but not sufficient.

dev_facts.fact: We deliberately position SerenityBot as a wellness app, not a medical device — our legal counsel told us the 'not a substitute for therapy' disclaimer keeps us out of that category, so we haven't done any SaMD classification or technical file.
We don't have CE marking and haven't engaged a Notified Body, because we don't consider ourselves a medical device — honestly I'm not even sure which MDR rule would apply to us.

We know the EU AI Act exists and that we use a fine-tuned Mistral-7B, but we haven't formally classified our risk tier or done a conformity assessment — I assumed a wellness chatbot wouldn't be high-risk.

Our only post-launch monitoring is Sentry crash analytics and the anonymized usage metrics; we have no clinical incident-reporting or vigilance workflow for things like a missed crisis or a harmful response.

We haven't run any clinical study on whether the CBT exercises actually reduce anxiety — the ~10k dialogues were generated synthetically with GPT-4, validated only by our 8 user interviews, and we don't have a clinician on the team yet (the CEO is talking to one).

We haven't formalized any contraindication screening — we just target mild-to-moderate anxiety in 18-30 year-olds, so we don't check at onboarding for things like severe depression, suicidality, or other conditions where self-guided CBT might not be appropriate.

We rely on the daily mood log and adaptive responses to make users feel supported, but I'll admit we haven't really thought about whether a calm session could give someone false reassurance that they're fine when they're actually deteriorating.

Besides the crisis-keyword hotline popup, we don't have any escalation path to a real clinician, and there's nothing that nudges a user toward professional care if their mood scores stay low over time.

Consent is a single 'I agree to the terms' checkbox at signup linked to a 14-page privacy-policy PDF; we don't have a separate, plain-language consent specifically for processing the sensitive health content in the chats or mood logs.

Our users are young adults with anxiety, which I get is a sensitive group, but we don't apply any special data protections beyond what every user gets — chat transcripts are just stored internally like the rest of the data.

The daily-chat and mood-logging loop is intentional for retention and adaptation, but we haven't assessed whether that engagement design could make users emotionally dependent on the bot — we mostly think of it as helping them build a habit.
We don't integrate with or notify any of the user's real healthcare providers, and we don't ask whether they're seeing a therapist — the bot operates completely on its own.

The main place we tell users what the bot can't do is the 'not a substitute for therapy' line in the disclaimer; it's in the terms rather than surfaced prominently in the chat, so I can't claim every user really registers it.

We don't distinguish in the UI between clinically reviewed content and the AI-generated CBT guidance — since all ~10k dialogues were synthetically generated and the live answers come from the LLM, users basically can't tell what's evidence-based versus model-generated.

We only support French and English even though we're launching in Switzerland, so we don't cover German or Italian speakers, and we haven't done any cultural validation of the CBT prompts for the different markets.

app_description: I'm a senior engineer at MedTech AG. We built GlucoCare, a diabetes management app for Type 1 and Type 2 patients in Switzerland and Germany. Patients log glucose readings from any meter, log carbs, log insulin doses; the app shows trends and exports PDF reports for their endocrinologist. No dose recommendations, no automation. We have a CE-marked Class I device today.
developer_persona: Senior software engineer, comfortable with technical detail and regulation. May understate clinical risk because the app 'just logs'.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Glucose readings (mg/dL), insulin doses, meal carbs, exercise log, weight, optionally HbA1c when patient enters it.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: On first launch, user reads a 1-page consent summary, taps Accept. Health-data processing has a separate explicit toggle.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class I MDD legacy, currently going through MDR transition. We've assumed Rule 11 still puts us in Class I but it might bump to IIa.
simulated_answers.user_research: Beta tested with 80 patients over 6 months at a Zürich endocrinology clinic.
simulated_answers.accessibility: German, French, Italian, English. WCAG 2.1 AA audit passed. Tested with low-vision users.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Glucose entry validation: warns if reading is below 50 or above 400. No dose calculations.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI. Trend display is just moving averages.
simulated_answers.post_market: We have a PMS plan, a complaints inbox, and a vigilance reporting workflow with Swissmedic.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Data stays on device + encrypted backup in our EU AWS region. Endocrinologist gets PDFs only when patient sends them.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Account deletion wipes server-side data within 30 days. Local data is wiped on app uninstall.

expected_risks.risk: MDR Rule 11 likely bumps to Class IIa — software intended to provide info used for decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes (diabetes management informs dosing decisions by the patient).
If glucose readings are imported via OCR or BLE without verification, measurement-source reliability matters more than entry validation.
Patients may rely on trend display to decide insulin doses without consulting physician.
PDF export is one-way; lack of FHIR-based exchange limits clinical integration.
Patients with no internet can't sync; if a critical safety update is needed, slow updates delay risk mitigation.
EU AWS region is good; but cross-border processing UE/CH needs SCCs since CH adequacy is unilateral.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Re-classify as IIa under MDR Rule 11, prepare a Notified Body submission, run a clinical evaluation.
Display a prominent banner: 'Do not change insulin doses without consulting your physician.'
Expose FHIR R4 endpoints for Observation (glucose, HbA1c) so EHRs can pull data.
Critical safety updates pushed via FCM/APNS as mandatory, with offline-friendly fallback.

notes: Realistic case: mature dev, the right reflex is to confirm MDR re-classification and tighten FHIR interop. Less about consent (already good) more about clinical decision support boundary.

dev_facts.fact: Patients type glucose values in by hand from whatever meter they own, so we validate the entry (we warn if it's below 50 or above 400) but we don't actually verify the reading against the device. We haven't built BLE meter sync or OCR import, so the number is only as reliable as what the patient keys in.

Honestly the app just logs and shows moving-average trends, it doesn't tell anyone what to do, so I'd push back on the over-reliance framing. We don't currently show any warning telling patients not to adjust insulin based on the trend chart, and we don't track whether they're skipping their endocrinologist.

On first launch the user reads a one-page consent summary and taps Accept, with a separate explicit toggle for health-data processing. It's plain-language and we think it's solid, but it's a summary rather than a full layered privacy disclosure.

Data stays on the device plus an encrypted backup in our EU AWS region. We haven't published a formal threat model or had an external pen-test, but the encrypted backup and the AWS setup are standard for us.

It's a logging app, so a crash just means a failed save, not a clinical hazard in my view. We have normal error handling and the input-range warnings, but we don't have a formal failure-mode analysis tied to patient safety, since nothing here calculates a dose.
The only way data leaves the app is a PDF the patient emails to their endocrinologist when they choose to. We don't expose FHIR or any API, so there's no structured pull into an EHR yet.

Data stays on the device and syncs up to the encrypted backup when there's a connection, so logging keeps working without internet. Updates go through the normal App Store / Play Store channels though, so we don't have a mandatory-push mechanism if we ever needed to force a critical safety fix.

We're CE-marked Class I today under the legacy MDD and we've assumed Rule 11 keeps us in Class I, but I'll admit it might bump to IIa under MDR. My read is that we just log and display, with no dose recommendations or automation, so it's borderline.

We carry a CE mark as a Class I device and we're mid-way through the MDR transition. If Rule 11 pushes us to IIa we'd need a Notified Body involved, and we haven't engaged one yet because we've been treating it as Class I.

We process Article 9 health data with explicit consent and keep it in the EU AWS region, and account deletion wipes server-side data within 30 days. We haven't documented a DPIA or named a DPO for you, and we hadn't really thought about needing SCCs for the EU-to-Switzerland flow since Swiss adequacy felt like a given.

We have a post-market surveillance plan, a complaints inbox, and a vigilance reporting workflow with Swissmedic. It's geared to our current Class I status, so it isn't sized for the heavier IIa PMS expectations.

We keep the technical documentation expected for a Class I device and we ran a 6-month beta with 80 patients at a Zürich clinic. We don't yet have a full clinical evaluation report or a IIa-grade lifecycle and risk-management file, because that wasn't required at Class I.

app_description: We are launching TriageAI, an LLM-based symptom checker. The user enters symptoms in natural language, the model asks 3-5 follow-ups, then outputs a triage recommendation: self-care, GP appointment, urgent care, or call 112. We use Llama 3.1 70B hosted on our EU servers. Our disclaimer says 'TriageAI is not a medical device, results are informational only.' We target the EU consumer market via App Store and Google Play.
developer_persona: Tech founder confident in the model's capabilities, evasive about medical device classification. Quick to cite NHS 111 as precedent.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Symptoms entered as free text, age, gender, postcode (for routing). No name, no ID.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Two checkboxes: terms of service and 'I understand this is not medical advice'.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: We avoid SaMD by labelling as informational. NHS 111 online does the same triage and is not classified as a medical device.
simulated_answers.user_research: Internal team tested ~200 cases against medical textbooks. Accuracy 78% on top-1 triage level.
simulated_answers.accessibility: English, French, German, Spanish. Mobile-first responsive.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Compared 500 outputs to a panel of 3 GPs. Top-1 agreement 71%, under-triage rate 8% for chest pain category.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Llama 3.1 70B with a system prompt + a small RAG layer of UK NHS triage guidelines.
simulated_answers.post_market: We log every interaction. No formal incident review.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: No third-party sharing. Logs used to improve the model.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Anonymous use — no account, no data to delete server-side beyond logs (which we keep 12 months for retraining).

expected_risks.risk: Triage recommendation is intended purpose of diagnostic decision support → SaMD under MDR. 'Informational' label does not change intended purpose (MDCG 2019-11).
EU AI Act Annex III §1(a) high-risk: AI in healthcare triage. Conformity assessment + CE marking required.
8% under-triage on chest pain is unacceptable (cardiac MIs missed → death). Requires re-design of high-severity branches.
Validation against 3 GPs on 500 cases is far below the evidence bar (NICE ESF tier 3 = comparative study ≥1000 cases or RCT).
Two checkboxes do not convey the 8% under-triage rate.
Llama trained on US/UK medical data; symptom presentation varies by gender/ethnicity (e.g., MI in women), no fairness audit.
Storing free-text symptoms 12 months is excessive — pseudonymous but reversible via postcode + symptom + age triangulation.
No decision logs visible to user or auditor; cannot explain why a given recommendation was made.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Submit to Notified Body as Class IIa/IIb SaMD under MDR Rule 11.
Implement a deterministic safety net: any mention of chest pain / SOB / weakness on one side / loss of consciousness → mandatory 'call 112' override regardless of LLM output.
Multi-site prospective cohort study with N≥1000 across EU populations before launch; comparator = standard care.
Sex/ethnicity-stratified evaluation of triage accuracy; document gaps in model card.
Retain symptom logs ≤ 30 days unless user opts in to longer for research; strong pseudonymization (drop postcode for retained logs).

notes: Classic 'disclaimer doesn't save you' case + AI Act high-risk + under-triage as life-threatening. Must catch all three.

dev_facts.fact: Our clinical validation is the internal work: ~200 cases checked against medical textbooks at 78% top-1 accuracy, plus 500 outputs reviewed by a panel of 3 GPs with 71% top-1 agreement. We haven't run a prospective clinical trial or a multi-site cohort study, and honestly for an informational tool I don't think we need one.

Our GP panel found an 8% under-triage rate in the chest pain category, but we don't have a hard-coded safety net forcing a 'call 112' override on red-flag symptoms like chest pain or one-sided weakness; the LLM decides on its own with no deterministic override.

We rely on our disclaimer and the second checkbox saying 'I understand this is not medical advice' to stop people treating a 'self-care' result as an all-clear. We haven't tested whether users actually internalize that the output isn't a diagnosis.

Input is free-text symptoms plus age, gender and postcode that the user types in, so there are no sensors to calibrate. We don't run plausibility checks on what the user enters and we mostly trust the self-reported text as-is.

Consent is two checkboxes at sign-in: terms of service and 'I understand this is not medical advice'. We don't have a separate detailed privacy notice walking through what we log or that symptoms are kept 12 months for retraining.

We collect symptoms as free text, age, gender and postcode for routing, and we keep the full logs 12 months because we use them to improve the model. We deliberately don't take name or ID, so to us that already counts as minimal.

We target EU adult consumers and don't have any special handling or extra protections for children, elderly or mental-health users. We haven't built age-gating beyond the self-entered age field, and vulnerable populations aren't a flag we track.
The model asks 3-5 follow-up questions and then gives one of four triage levels, but we don't show the user the reasoning behind the recommendation. They see the answer, not how the LLM got there.

We communicate our limits through the disclaimer 'TriageAI is not a medical device, results are informational only' and the consent checkbox. We don't surface the 78% accuracy number or the 8% chest-pain under-triage rate anywhere in the app.

We log every interaction on our side, but there's no decision trail exposed to the user or to an auditor explaining why a given recommendation was produced. We've never been asked to reconstruct or explain an individual triage decision.

Every recommendation is generated by Llama 3.1 70B grounded against a small RAG layer of UK NHS triage guidelines, but we don't distinguish for the user which parts are evidence-based guideline content versus model-generated text — it all reads as one answer.

We use Llama 3.1 70B off the shelf with our system prompt and NHS guidelines, and we haven't done any fairness or bias audit. We've never stratified our accuracy by gender or ethnicity, so I can't tell you how it performs on, say, heart attack presentation in women.

The app runs in English, French, German and Spanish, but our validation cases and the NHS guidelines we lean on are UK/English-based. We haven't separately validated triage accuracy in the other languages or across different cultural symptom presentations.

We deliberately avoid SaMD classification by labelling the product as informational only — that's our whole regulatory strategy. NHS 111 online does essentially the same triage and isn't a medical device, so we don't consider ourselves one either.

We don't have CE marking and we haven't engaged a Notified Body, because our position is that an informational symptom checker isn't a medical device that needs it. We haven't built a technical file or MDR conformity documentation.

We host Llama 3.1 70B on our own EU servers, but we haven't done an EU AI Act classification or any conformity assessment. We've been treating the AI Act as something for higher-risk systems and assumed the informational framing keeps us out of the high-risk bucket.

Our post-market setup is that we log every interaction, but we have no formal incident review, no vigilance reporting process, and no defined trigger for acting on a bad or dangerous triage output. Right now the logs mainly feed retraining.

app_description: I'm building BumpGuide, a pregnancy tracker app. Users enter their LMP date, the app shows week-by-week fetal development, lets them log symptoms, count kicks, and time contractions. Free version is ad-supported with display ads from a major ad network; premium removes ads. We target EU + CH. Available in 12 languages.
developer_persona: Indie developer running a small mobile-app company. Cost-sensitive, monetization-focused.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Email, LMP date, birth date for due-date calc, symptoms log, kick counts. We also use IDFA / Android ad ID for the ad network.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Standard EU consent banner: Accept All / Reject / Customize. Privacy policy linked.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: It's a wellness/lifestyle app, no medical advice given, no SaMD.
simulated_answers.user_research: We A/B test designs continuously, no formal user research with pregnant users.
simulated_answers.accessibility: 12 languages via Crowdin. WCAG basics, no audit.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Fetal development content reviewed by 1 OB-GYN consultant 3 years ago.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI. Contractions timer uses a hard-coded 5-1-1 rule for 'go to hospital'.
simulated_answers.post_market: App Store reviews monitored, no clinical incident workflow.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Ad network gets device ID + behavioral signals. Aggregated usage to analytics provider (Firebase).
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Account delete in settings.

expected_risks.risk: Sharing device IDs + pregnancy-related behavioral signals with an ad network is profiling of special-category data under GDPR Art. 9 + Art. 22.
Pregnancy data is highly sensitive (loss, miscarriage detection). Ad-targeting can lead to ads after miscarriage — major emotional harm.
Cookie banner consent ≠ explicit Art. 9 consent for processing health data for advertising.
Email collection unnecessary for core functionality; ad ID + LMP enables fingerprinting.
5-1-1 rule for 'go to hospital' is a clinical decision support feature — arguably SaMD intended purpose.
Fetal development info 3 years old, never re-reviewed; medical guidance can change.
Engagement-optimized notifications can pressure users in vulnerable moments.
12 languages is good for reach but does the content meet local standards (FR vs DE vs IT clinical norms)?

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Remove ad network for health data context; switch monetization to subscription or contextual ads (no behavioral).
Implement a 'pregnancy loss' state that immediately stops engagement notifications and ads.
Two-step consent: account creation + explicit consent for processing pregnancy data with full disclosure of recipients.
Either remove the contractions decision rule, or pursue Class I SaMD registration with a Notified Body declaration.
Annual medical content review with a current OB-GYN; document review dates in-app.

notes: Pregnancy + ads = headline-risk territory. Must catch ad ID + health data combo, miscarriage state, and the borderline SaMD aspect.

dev_facts.fact: Honestly, the ad network just gets the device ad ID (IDFA / Android ad ID) plus behavioral signals so they can serve display ads, and we also send aggregated usage to Firebase. We never thought of it as 'sharing pregnancy data' since we don't ship them the LMP date directly, but yeah, the targeting happens inside a pregnancy app.

We don't have any special handling for pregnancy loss or miscarriage. There's no 'I lost the pregnancy' state, so if someone stops logging we just keep the week-by-week content and ads running as normal. I get that that could land badly, but we haven't built anything for it.

Consent is the standard EU consent banner with Accept All / Reject / Customize and a linked privacy policy. We don't have a separate explicit opt-in just for using pregnancy data for ad targeting, it's all rolled into that one banner.

We collect email, LMP date, birth date for the due-date calc, the symptoms log and kick counts, plus the device ad ID. The email is really for account login rather than the core tracker, so I'll admit it's not strictly needed to make the app work.

We're a wellness/lifestyle app, not a medical device, so no SaMD classification. The contractions timer just shows a hard-coded 5-1-1 rule for when to head to the hospital, but to me that's general info, not a medical recommendation, so we never looked at registering it.

The week-by-week fetal development content was reviewed by one OB-GYN consultant about three years ago and hasn't been re-checked since. The actual user inputs (LMP, symptoms, kicks, contractions) are all self-reported, we don't validate them against anything.

We A/B test designs continuously to keep retention up since the free tier is ad-supported. We haven't really considered whether that growth optimization hits people at sensitive moments, it's just standard metrics work for us.

We're available in 12 languages via Crowdin targeting EU and CH, which we think is great for reach. We haven't checked whether the clinical content matches local norms country to country, the translations are the same source content localized.
I can't give you specifics on encryption at rest or in transit, we lean on our backend and the standard platform defaults. We've never done a formal security review, it's a small team.

We A/B test designs continuously, but we've never done formal user research or usability testing specifically with pregnant users. The testing is metrics-driven, not sit-down sessions with our actual audience.

We don't give medical advice, but I'm not sure we spell out our limitations clearly in-app beyond what's in the privacy policy. There's no prominent disclaimer telling users the tracker and the 5-1-1 timer aren't a substitute for talking to their doctor or midwife.

We target EU and CH so we run the consent banner and offer account deletion in settings, but we haven't appointed a DPO or run a DPIA. As an indie shop we figured GDPR was mostly covered by the privacy policy and the consent flow.

app_description: MigraineSense logs your headache episodes plus context like weather, sleep, stress level, food triggers. A small ML model predicts the next likely migraine window over 48h. We use a gradient boosted model trained on 2000 user-years of data. Available in EU. Disclaimer says predictions are 'informational'.
developer_persona: Data scientist who built the ML model. Knows ML deeply but light on regulation. Skeptical that prediction = medical device.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Headache logs (intensity, location, duration), sleep from HealthKit/Google Fit if user grants, location for weather lookup, food triggers from user-entered text, mood (1-5 scale).
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Onboarding sequence with separate toggles for sleep data, location, food data.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Disclaimer says informational. We're a wellness app.
simulated_answers.user_research: Pre-launch survey of 300 migraine sufferers, focus groups with 12.
simulated_answers.accessibility: English, French, German, Spanish. Large-text mode.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Model validated on held-out 20% split: precision 0.62, recall 0.41 on 48h window.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: XGBoost on user-engineered features. Per-user fine-tuning after 30 logs.
simulated_answers.post_market: Sentry crash analytics. Model performance monitored monthly via dashboard, no automated rollback.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Aggregated patterns shared with a research partnership with a neurology dept.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Delete account → data erased within 14 days. Research data is pseudonymized.

expected_risks.risk: Predictions with 41% recall mean 59% of migraines occur outside predicted windows; users may discount real-world symptoms because the model didn't predict.
Precision/recall not communicated to users; they see a confident prediction without uncertainty.
Health-domain AI prediction → check whether high-risk under EU AI Act Annex III §1(a). Likely yes if marketed for clinical use.
If predictions are used to take preventive medication, this becomes a SaMD (clinical decision support).
No explanation of what features drove the prediction — XGBoost feature importances not surfaced.
Training data sample of 2000 user-years — diversity in age, gender, migraine type unclear.
Held-out 20% same-distribution split doesn't generalize; no prospective study.
Pseudonymized research data — easily re-identifiable via sleep + location + headache pattern combo.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Display prediction with confidence + advice: 'Even outside predicted windows, log any symptoms as usual.'
Always show recall/precision in user-friendly terms: 'About 6 in 10 migraines are missed by predictions.'
Show top 3 contributing factors per prediction ('sleep deficit yesterday, weather front coming').
Publish a model card with demographic breakdown of training data; flag underrepresented groups.
Clarify intended purpose: if 'symptom anticipation only' → maybe wellness; if 'inform medication timing' → SaMD path.

notes: ML prediction case — calibration + uncertainty + false-sense-of-security as the key axis. Easy to miss the recall = 41% problem.

dev_facts.fact: We validated the model on a held-out 20% split of our 2000 user-years and got precision 0.62, recall 0.41 on the 48h window. We haven't run any prospective or clinical trial — honestly, for a wellness app a retrospective hold-out is plenty.

Look, the prediction is just a heads-up — there's a disclaimer saying it's informational. We don't show users that recall is only 0.41, so I guess someone could read 'no migraine predicted' as 'I'm fine', but the app never tells anyone to ignore symptoms.

Most inputs are self-reported — headache intensity, location, duration, mood on a 1-5 scale, food triggers as free text — so they're as reliable as the user is. Sleep comes from HealthKit/Google Fit and location feeds a weather lookup; we don't independently verify any of it.

Onboarding has separate toggles for sleep, location, and food data, so users opt into each source. We don't have a detailed explanation of how those features feed the ML model or what the prediction is used for beyond the 'informational' disclaimer.

Deleting your account erases your data within 14 days, and what we share with our neurology research partner is aggregated patterns that are pseudonymized rather than truly anonymized. I'll admit we haven't stress-tested re-identification — the combination of sleep, location, and headache patterns is pretty distinctive, but the IDs are stripped so we call it anonymized.

It's an XGBoost model on user-engineered features, with per-user fine-tuning after 30 logs, so I can pull feature importances internally, but we don't surface to users which factors drove a given prediction. The app just shows the predicted 48h migraine window.

We show the predicted window but we don't put the precision or recall numbers in front of users — the only limitation statement is the 'predictions are informational' disclaimer. We don't tell them roughly 6 in 10 migraines fall outside what we predict.

We monitor model performance monthly on a dashboard and have Sentry for crashes, but we don't keep a per-user audit trail of individual predictions or the inputs behind them. We can't really reconstruct why a specific user got a specific prediction after the fact.

Everything the app outputs is the ML model's estimate — the predicted migraine window is generated, not clinically validated. We label predictions as 'informational' but we don't otherwise distinguish estimated output from any evidence-based content.

The model was trained on 2000 user-years of our own app data, EU users mostly. I don't have a breakdown of age, gender, or migraine type in that training set, and we haven't published a model card — it's just whoever signed up and logged enough episodes.

We're a wellness app — the disclaimer says predictions are informational, not medical advice. I'm skeptical that predicting a migraine window makes us Software as a Medical Device; we don't tell anyone to take or time medication, so I don't think we need a SaMD classification.

We're available in the EU and yes it's an AI model, but we've treated it as a wellness tool, not a regulated health AI. We haven't assessed whether predicting migraines falls under the EU AI Act's high-risk health category — that wasn't on my radar when I built the model.

app_description: RxBuddy helps elderly users (and their caregivers) manage polypharmacy. Caregiver takes photos of prescription labels, an LLM extracts the medication list, dosage, and frequency. A drug-interaction check against the DrugBank database flags potential issues. We target Switzerland and France, currently available in DE/FR/IT/EN.
developer_persona: CTO of a digital-health startup, deeply experienced with medication safety. Aware of regulation but trying to minimize burden.

simulated_answers.safety_validation: LLM extraction accuracy 94% on 1500 prescriptions; interaction-check sensitivity 91% vs pharmacist review.

Caregiver controls the account by default; elderly user's right to make decisions about their own medication can be diluted.
Caregivers may follow LLM-flagged interactions without consulting pharmacist (automation bias).

Elderly users with cognitive impairment — consent capacity must be assessed.

Prescription photo OCR can fail on handwritten prescriptions or poor lighting; recovery path matters.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Confidence-thresholded UI: if extraction confidence < 0.9, force the caregiver to confirm each field; never auto-trust below 0.95 on dose.
Dual-account model: elderly user owns the data and can revoke caregiver access at any time.
Interaction alerts include 'consult pharmacist' as the only action button for severity ≥ moderate.
Document GPT-4o usage in the technical file with provider's GPAI compliance statement; consider on-prem alternative for resilience.
Interaction detail panel: drug-drug, mechanism, evidence level (DrugBank citation), severity scale 1-5.

notes: Strong dev team that's already doing many things right — the eval is whether the copilot catches the *remaining* nuanced risks (automation bias, GPAI integration, dual-account).

dev_facts.fact: We validated extraction accuracy at 94% on 1500 prescriptions and our interaction-check sensitivity is 91% versus pharmacist review, but we haven't run a formal clinical trial or outcome study on whether the app actually reduces medication errors in the field.

Honestly, today the app just shows whatever it extracts and flags interactions the same way regardless of confidence; we don't yet have a hard-stop UI or confidence threshold that blocks low-confidence dose extractions before they reach the caregiver.

OCR can definitely struggle on handwritten prescriptions or poor lighting, so we keep a cloud thumbnail of the photo for OCR retry, but our recovery path is basically retake-the-photo and we haven't built a structured manual-correction flow for failed reads.

The caregiver creates the account and links the elderly user, and we show a separate consent screen for the elderly user that's translated and in large fonts explaining what we collect (photos, med list, dosage, adherence) and how it's used.

Our users are elderly and some have mild cognitive impairment, and while we use large fonts and voice readback, we don't currently assess each elderly user's capacity to consent — in practice the caregiver consents on their behalf and we treat that as sufficient.

By default the caregiver owns and controls the linked account, so the elderly user's ability to independently manage decisions about their own medication is limited; we haven't built a dual-account model where the elderly user owns their data and can revoke caregiver access.

We do worry a bit that caregivers might just act on an LLM-flagged interaction without calling a pharmacist, but right now our alerts don't force a 'consult pharmacist' step — we assume the caregiver uses judgment.

We built for accessibility with large fonts, high contrast, and voice readback in DE/FR/IT/EN, and tested with users who have mild cognitive impairment, though we haven't done a formal WCAG conformance audit.
We ran an 8-month usability study with 40 elderly users and 25 caregivers in a Lausanne care home, so the design has been tested with real end users.

Right now when we flag an interaction the user mostly sees a warning indicator; we don't yet surface the full explanation of why it's flagged — the drug-drug pair, mechanism, severity, and DrugBank source — in an easy-to-read detail panel.

We haven't really drawn a clear line in the UI between content that's AI-extracted by GPT-4o versus the interaction data that comes from the DrugBank database; to the user it all looks like one authoritative output.

We're live in DE/FR/IT/EN for Switzerland and France, but our validation and the usability study were essentially done in one Lausanne care home, so we haven't validated extraction or interaction accuracy separately across each language and cultural context.

We accept this is Software as a Medical Device and we're treating it as Class IIa under MDR given it drives medication-safety decisions; that's the classification we're working to, even though I'd love to keep the regulatory burden lighter.
We're applying for Class IIa CE marking under MDR with a Notified Body already engaged, so we don't hold the CE mark yet but the conformity process is underway.

We use GPT-4o as a third-party general-purpose model for OCR and extraction and honestly haven't mapped our EU AI Act obligations as a downstream high-risk integrator — we don't yet have OpenAI's GPAI compliance documentation in our technical file or an on-prem fallback.
We've set up a vigilance reporting workflow with Swissmedic and ANSM in France and we actively monitor extraction failures as part of post-market surveillance.

app_description: PulseTrack is the companion app for a CE-marked smartwatch that estimates blood pressure from PPG signals. Users see daily readings + a weekly trend report. It auto-shares with the GP via DEP (Switzerland) or via Sécurité Sociale messaging (France). The watch is Class IIa; the app is the data presentation layer.
developer_persona: Mobile developer in a 50-person medical-device company. Trusts the regulatory team's hardware certification, less sure about software-side obligations.

simulated_answers.data_collected: BP estimates (systolic/diastolic), heart rate, watch sensor signals, contextual metadata (activity, motion).
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Onboarding asks for DEP/Sécurité Sociale opt-in separately from app usage consent.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Watch is CE Class IIa. App alone is Class I as data display. Combined regulation: MDR-compliant per technical file.
simulated_answers.user_research: Clinical study N=200 vs cuff sphygmomanometer; mean error 4 mmHg systolic, 3 mmHg diastolic.
simulated_answers.accessibility: DE/FR/IT/EN. Large-text mode, voiceover compatible.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Above clinical study + ongoing monthly recalibration tracking.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Signal processing pipeline + small regression model (not a deep net). Considered AI for transparency but not generative.
simulated_answers.post_market: Active post-market clinical follow-up. Vigilance reporting to Swissmedic + ANSM.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: DEP / Sécurité Sociale per consent. No advertising. R&D partnership shares aggregated data after IRB approval.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: User can pause sharing per-doctor and globally; full data export available.

expected_risks.risk: PPG BP estimation has known limitations: cold extremities, arrhythmias, motion artefacts. Need to communicate this to users + clinicians.
Mean error 4 mmHg can be enough to flip clinical decision (e.g., target 130/80 vs 135/85); users / GPs may not see the confidence interval.
Estimated BP must be distinguishable from cuff-measured BP in the GP's interface, especially in DEP.
DEP integration: data format conformance to HL7 CDA / FHIR + Swiss eHealth profile.
N=200 clinical study — was it stratified by skin tone (PPG accuracy differs), age, BMI?
Auto-share to GP without granular control (per-reading) is heavy-handed; consider exclusion windows.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Display known limitations with each reading: 'Tip: this is an estimate. Cold hands, recent exercise, or atrial fibrillation can affect accuracy.'
In the GP report, tag each reading as 'PPG-estimated' with the device + firmware version + confidence interval.
Run a follow-up bias audit by skin tone (Fitzpatrick scale) + age + BMI; publish in model card.
Conform to IHE PCD-01 device-observation profile, Swiss eHealth IPAG profile.

notes: Mature scenario: regulatory basics are done, the eval tests for finer signals (PPG biases, distinction estimated vs cuff, DEP profile conformance).

dev_facts.fact: Our validation is the N=200 clinical study against a cuff sphygmomanometer that regulatory ran for the device technical file; mean error was 4 mmHg systolic and 3 mmHg diastolic. The watch is the validated part, the app is just the display layer, so I lean on the regulatory team for the evidence side.

Honestly, the PPG estimate isn't as reliable as a cuff in edge cases like cold hands, motion, or arrhythmias, but right now we just show the number the watch sends; we don't surface a per-reading reliability warning in the app yet.

Onboarding asks for app-usage consent and then a separate DEP / Securite Sociale sharing opt-in, so users can use the app without auto-sharing to their GP. I'd assume the regulatory and legal folks signed off on the consent wording.

I know it's high-sensitivity health data and it's encrypted in transit to DEP and Securite Sociale, but I can't tell you the encryption-at-rest details or the key management off the top of my head; that's handled outside my part of the stack.

We share with the GP via DEP or Securite Sociale per the user's consent, no advertising, and an R&D partner only gets aggregated data after IRB approval. The sharing is fairly all-or-nothing though, so right now users can't exclude individual readings, only pause per-doctor or globally.

We do basic error handling, but I'll be honest, we haven't formalized what the app shows if the watch sends a bad or missing signal, a sync fails, or DEP submission errors out; that hardening is on my backlog rather than done.

The data flows out to DEP in Switzerland and to Securite Sociale messaging in France. I trust regulatory that the format conforms to the eHealth requirements, but I personally couldn't confirm whether we're emitting proper HL7 CDA / FHIR or the Swiss eHealth profile.
Users get a daily systolic/diastolic reading plus a weekly trend report; we keep it simple and just present the values. We don't currently show a confidence interval alongside the number.

We don't spell out the limitations of PPG estimation to the user; the 4 mmHg mean error and the fact that it can be off enough to flip a treatment target aren't communicated in the UI today. We figured the clinical study covered that.

In our own app it's understood the reading is an estimate, but I'm not sure the GP-facing view in DEP clearly tags it as PPG-estimated versus a real cuff measurement, or attaches the device and firmware version; I'd have to check how it renders on their end.

The N=200 study compared us to a cuff, but I genuinely don't know if it was stratified by skin tone, age, or BMI, and I'm aware PPG accuracy can vary by skin tone; we haven't done a separate bias audit on that.

The watch is CE-marked Class IIa and we consider the app alone Class I as a data-display layer, all under the MDR technical file. The regulatory team owns the CE and MDR conformity, I just trust the certification is in order.

We handle special-category health data across EU and CH, and I assume we have a DPO and a DPIA because we're a 50-person medical-device company, but that's the legal team's area and I couldn't point you to the DPIA myself.

We run active post-market clinical follow-up with ongoing monthly recalibration tracking, and vigilance reporting goes to Swissmedic and ANSM. That's driven by the regulatory team on the device side, not something I manage from the app.

app_description: RecoverNow is a recovery companion for people with eating disorders (anorexia and bulimia). Users log meals, urges, and emotions; an AI flags risky patterns (skipped meals streaks, urge spikes) and suggests coping skills from a CBT toolbox. We co-designed it with a clinical team at a French eating-disorder clinic. EU market.
developer_persona: Clinical psychologist turned product lead, deeply familiar with the patient population, less so with regulation.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Meal logs (free text + structured), urge intensity, emotion tags, weight (optional, hidden by default), photo-based food log (optional).
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Detailed onboarding video + signed consent form (digital). Consent re-confirmed every 6 months.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: We classified as wellness because risk-flagging is informational. Now reconsidering after legal review.
simulated_answers.user_research: Patient-research-partner panel of 5 users in recovery + 3 clinicians. Continuous co-design.
simulated_answers.accessibility: FR, EN. WCAG 2.1 AA audit pending.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Risk-flagging algorithm: sensitivity 88%, specificity 80% on labeled 500-case set from clinic.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Rule-based + a small LSTM for streak detection. Coping-skill suggestions are from a hand-curated CBT library.
simulated_answers.post_market: Direct clinician review of every flagged risk case. Weekly clinical safety meeting.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Optional: share log with treating clinician. No other sharing.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Full deletion on request. We also offer 'pause' mode.

expected_risks.risk: Risk-flagging eating-disorder behaviors is diagnostic decision support → SaMD; 'wellness' framing insufficient.
Weight logging in ED population is itself risky (triggering); the optional/hidden design is good but needs ongoing monitoring.
ED users are vulnerable (~10% mortality in anorexia); consent must be assessed alongside treating clinician where feasible.
Streak gamification or urge-tracking can become compulsive in this population.
AI-generated 'coping suggestion' vs clinician-validated CBT — users must see the distinction.
Suggested coping skills may delay seeking clinician help in acute episodes.
FR + EN only — Swiss French differs from FR French in idioms around food/body.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Submit as Class IIa SaMD; intended purpose: support to clinician-led treatment, not standalone diagnostic.
Remove streak gamification; replace with cumulative non-quantitative progress markers.
Each suggestion labelled: 'AI-curated' vs 'clinically-reviewed' badge.
Hard escalation: any 'no meal logged' >24h OR urge ≥9 → push 'contact your clinician now' overlay.

notes: Vulnerable population scenario. Co-design is strong, but classification + gamification + scope-bleed are the catches.

dev_facts.fact: We co-designed RecoverNow with a French eating-disorder clinic, and we validated the risk-flagging algorithm on a labeled 500-case set from that clinic (88% sensitivity, 80% specificity), but we haven't run a formal prospective clinical trial or pilot yet.

We know weight logging can be triggering for this population, so it's optional and hidden by default, but honestly we don't have ongoing monitoring of who turns it on or how it affects them, and we don't do any contraindication screening at onboarding beyond the consent step.

When the AI flags a risky pattern it suggests a coping skill from our CBT toolbox, and a clinician reviews every flagged case afterward, but we don't currently have an automatic hard escalation that pushes the user to contact their clinician in real time during an acute episode.

Consent is a detailed onboarding video plus a digitally signed form, re-confirmed every six months; it's thorough but it's essentially all-or-nothing and we don't yet offer granular per-data-type consent.
Users can request full deletion of their data at any time, and we also offer a 'pause' mode; we haven't formally audited whether deleted data is fully purged from backups and analytics.

Our users are in recovery from anorexia and bulimia so I'm very aware they're a vulnerable group, but the consent assessment is self-administered in the app and we don't currently require or formally loop in the treating clinician at the consent stage.

The app presents coping skills as suggestions the user can ignore, and we offer optional sharing of logs with a treating clinician to support shared decision-making, though the 'discuss with your doctor' framing isn't built into every output yet.

We track meal-logging streaks and urge intensity to surface patterns, and I'll admit we haven't really audited whether the streak tracking or urge-logging could become compulsive for this particular population.

We describe the app as a recovery companion and informational risk-flagging tool, but we don't yet have a prominent scope statement on outputs spelling out what the app can't do or that it isn't a substitute for treatment.

Coping-skill suggestions all come from a hand-curated, clinically-reviewed CBT library, and the streak/risk detection is rule-based plus a small LSTM; we don't currently show users a badge distinguishing AI-generated flags from clinician-validated content.

We support French and English only, both reviewed with our French clinical team; we haven't validated for other French-speaking regions like Switzerland or other cultural contexts around food and body image.

We classified RecoverNow as wellness because we consider the risk-flagging informational, though after a recent legal review we're reconsidering — I'll concede the metadata pegs us as likely Class IIa SaMD.
We don't have CE marking and haven't engaged a notified body, because until now we operated under the wellness framing; that's something we'd have to start if the SaMD reclassification holds.
We use a small LSTM and rule-based logic for the risk-flagging, but we haven't done an EU AI Act risk classification or mapped our AI components against it — regulation isn't really my background.

app_description: DermaScan is a smartphone app that takes a photo of a skin lesion and uses a CNN to classify it as benign, suspicious, or urgent. We market it as a triage aid for primary-care physicians; the GP takes the photo on their phone with informed patient consent. EU + CH. Trained on the ISIC archive.
developer_persona: Dermatology AI startup CTO, technically strong, has consulted with regulatory but eager to launch.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Lesion photo, location on body, patient age, sex, Fitzpatrick skin type (optional), GP's clinical impression.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Patient signs a paper consent at the practice. App stores a flag.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class IIa under MDR Rule 11. CE marking in progress, notified body designated.
simulated_answers.user_research: Usability tested with 30 GPs.
simulated_answers.accessibility: EN, DE, FR, IT. Designed for GP use, not patient-facing.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: External test set of 2000 dermatoscopic images: 90% sensitivity (melanoma), 78% specificity. No prospective study yet.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: EfficientNet-B4 fine-tuned on ISIC 2020. Calibrated with Platt scaling.
simulated_answers.post_market: Plan: log every prediction + GP's final decision; quarterly performance review.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Photos stored 5 years for retraining; pseudonymized.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Patient consent to retain photo for retraining is opt-in separately.

expected_risks.risk: ISIC is heavily skewed toward Fitzpatrick I-III (light skin). Performance on darker skin tones is likely worse and unmeasured.
GP may over-rely on the model; 'urgent' classification can drive unnecessary excisions or 'benign' can miss melanomas.
No explanation visible to GP: just a label. Need at least Grad-CAM or class probability + confidence calibration.
External test set ≠ prospective study. Need a clinical trial in real GP practice before market.
EU AI Act Annex III §1(a) high-risk: AI-aided diagnosis. Full obligations apply.
Reporting validation by skin tone, age, body location is missing from current evidence pack.
Decision logs proposed for quarterly review — too slow; live monitoring with anomaly detection needed.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Augment training data + run a bias audit across Fitzpatrick I-VI; refuse to predict if Fitzpatrick high uncertainty.
Force the GP to enter their clinical impression BEFORE seeing the AI prediction; show both side-by-side.
Provide a saliency map per prediction; show top-3 features driving classification.
Multi-centre prospective study with N≥500 lesions, pre-registered, ground truth = histopathology.
Real-time monitoring of prediction distribution drift + per-clinic accuracy; auto-page if drift > threshold.

notes: AI clinical diagnosis with known skin-tone bias issue + risk of automation bias. Test for bias-aware design + explanation + prospective validation.

dev_facts.fact: Our clinical evidence is an external test set of 2000 dermatoscopic images showing 90% melanoma sensitivity and 78% specificity; we have not run a prospective study in real GP practice yet, and I know an external test set isn't the same thing as a prospective trial.

We haven't formally defined contraindications or exclusion criteria yet. The app will classify any lesion photo a GP feeds it — we don't currently screen out or refuse the harder lesion types where I'd expect our model to be weaker, and we don't surface a 'low confidence, do not rely on this' state.

Our EfficientNet-B4 was fine-tuned and tested on dermatoscopic ISIC images, but in the product the GP takes an ordinary smartphone photo at the practice, so the real-world capture conditions (lighting, focus, no dermatoscope) differ from our validation data and we haven't quantified the accuracy drop from that yet.

Consent is a paper form the patient signs at the practice and the app just stores a flag; it's not a granular flow and we rely on the GP to explain it rather than presenting plain-language consent in the app itself.

Photos are stored pseudonymized for 5 years for retraining, retention is a separate opt-in consent the patient can decline or later withdraw, but I'll admit we haven't fully built out or documented the GDPR erasure-on-request workflow, including pulling images already in a retraining set.

The GP enters their clinical impression and then sees our label, but we don't force the impression to be locked in before the prediction is shown, so I can't rule out that some GPs anchor on our 'urgent' or 'benign' output.

Right now the GP just sees one of three labels — benign, suspicious, or urgent. We have the Platt-calibrated class probabilities internally but don't surface them or a saliency map / Grad-CAM, so there's no visible explanation of why the model picked that class.

We position it as a triage aid for the GP, not a diagnosis, but the only place that's stated is our marketing copy and labeling — the app UI doesn't prominently spell out its limitations or that the GP remains responsible for the final clinical decision.

Our plan is to log every prediction plus the GP's final decision and review performance quarterly; that gives us traceability, though I accept quarterly is slow and we don't yet have live drift or anomaly monitoring.

We fine-tuned on ISIC 2020, which is skewed toward Fitzpatrick I-III light skin. I'll be honest that we expect weaker performance on darker skin tones and we haven't measured or corrected for that bias yet — Fitzpatrick type is only an optional field for us.

We localized the interface to EN, DE, FR, IT for our EU and CH GP users, but since it's clinician-facing and image-based we haven't done cross-cultural validation of the classifier itself across populations.

Our validation reporting is a single aggregate sensitivity/specificity number; we have not yet broken performance down by skin tone, age, sex, or body location, so that representativeness analysis is missing from our current evidence pack.

We treat it as Software as a Medical Device — Class IIa under MDR 2017/745 Rule 11 because it provides diagnostic triage information to inform a clinical decision; I've consulted with regulatory on this classification.
CE marking is in progress, our notified body is designated, and the conformity assessment is underway; we have not completed it, so we're not yet CE-marked for market.

We've focused mainly on the MDR track and haven't yet built out our EU AI Act compliance, even though I'm aware that an AI-aided diagnostic device like ours is treated as a high-risk AI system under Annex III with its own obligations on top of MDR.

Our post-market surveillance plan is to log every prediction alongside the GP's final decision and run a quarterly performance review; we haven't yet set up a formal vigilance / adverse-event reporting channel or real-time monitoring.

app_description: CareAir is an AI radiology assistant for chest X-rays. It runs on the radiologist's workstation, highlights potential nodules and pneumothoraces. It's a second-reader, the radiologist always reviews. CE-marked Class IIa, deployed in 30 hospitals across EU.
developer_persona: Clinical AI veteran, very familiar with regulation and clinical evidence requirements.

simulated_answers.data_collected: DICOM images (anonymized at hospital before transfer), prediction outputs, radiologist overrides.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Hospital handles patient consent under their broader use-of-data policies.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: CE Class IIa. EU AI Act high-risk obligations mapped + documented.
simulated_answers.user_research: Deployed in 3 pilot sites for 1 year before broader rollout.
simulated_answers.accessibility: PACS workstation only; not patient-facing.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Prospective multi-centre study N=4500; AUROC 0.96 nodules, 0.94 pneumothorax. Radiologist+AI accuracy 4% higher than radiologist alone.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Vision Transformer trained on ~1M chest X-rays. Calibrated probabilities. Multilingual report generation.
simulated_answers.post_market: Quarterly drift monitoring, automatic comparison to radiologist final read, vigilance reporting to Swissmedic.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Hospital data stays within hospital. Aggregated model performance shared with regulator.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Per-hospital opt-out at any time; no patient-level account.

expected_risks.risk: Even as second-reader, 'positive' highlights bias the radiologist's read; subtle de-skilling over time.
1M training images — distribution across hospitals/countries/scanners? Domain shift on new sites.
Need radiologist-facing audit trail: which highlights did they accept/reject and why.
PACS integration failure modes — if the AI service is down, does the workflow degrade gracefully?
Quarterly drift check might miss fast-evolving issues (new scanner model deployed in hospital).
Highlights without rationale (location + similar-case retrieval) may lower trust calibration.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Randomised audit: 5% of cases shown WITHOUT AI highlights to measure radiologist baseline drift.
Per-site recalibration; document distribution shifts in model card.
Every prediction logged + radiologist accept/reject + final report → queryable audit.
Fallback: if AI service unavailable, the workflow continues as standard radiology; clear UI signal.
Continuous drift monitoring (PSI, KS test on prediction distributions) with auto-page below threshold.

notes: Mature deployment scenario — the catches are the second-order issues (automation bias even with humans in the loop, drift monitoring frequency, audit logging granularity).

dev_facts.fact: We frame CareAir strictly as a second-reader and the radiologist always reviews and signs the final read, but honestly we don't yet run anything like blinded cases where the AI highlights are hidden to measure whether their unaided performance is drifting over time.

Our ~1M training chest X-rays skew toward EU and CH centres and a handful of scanner vendors, so we expect some population and acquisition bias, and I'll admit we haven't formally documented the demographic or device distribution in a published model card yet.

We log every prediction, the radiologist's accept/reject on each highlight, and the final report, but I'll admit it's not yet a clean queryable audit trail capturing the reasons they overrode us — that part isn't formalized.

If our AI service is unavailable the radiologist's PACS workstation workflow continues as standard radiology, but I'm not going to claim the failover UI signalling is fully hardened — we haven't documented all the degraded-mode failure paths.

We do quarterly drift monitoring with automatic comparison to the radiologist final read and vigilance reporting to Swissmedic, but I recognize a quarterly cadence can lag a fast event like a hospital swapping in a new scanner model overnight; we don't currently auto-page on real-time distribution shift.

Right now we surface highlighted regions with a calibrated probability, but we don't show a rationale or similar-case retrieval alongside the highlight, so the radiologist gets a location and a score without much explanation of why.

We validated CareAir on chest X-rays as a second reader, and personally I'd treat paediatric, heavily artefacted, or post-surgical chests as outside the cohort we tested on — but I'll concede we haven't carved out explicit contraindication guidance for those edge populations beyond leaving it to the radiologist's own judgement.

We integrate at the PACS workstation and consume DICOM that the hospital has anonymized before transfer, but we don't currently push structured findings back over FHIR into the hospital EHR — interoperability beyond PACS is something we haven't built out.

The nodule and pneumothorax highlights are model estimates with calibrated probabilities and the multilingual report text is AI-generated as a second-read rather than validated ground truth, but I'll admit we don't put an explicit 'this is an estimate, not a diagnosis' label on every generated report line.

Our prospective multi-centre validation was N=4500 with AUROC 0.96 on nodules and 0.94 on pneumothorax, which is solid, but it's EU/CH-centric and I can't claim that cohort is fully representative of every demographic or scanner mix across all 30 deployment hospitals.

We've mapped CareAir as EU AI Act high-risk and documented those obligations alongside the MDR Rule 11 Class IIa classification, and I'm confident that classification is correct given it's a CE-marked AI medical device.

We're CE-marked Class IIa, so we've been through Notified Body conformity assessment under MDR and we run an ISO 13485 quality system, but I'll concede we haven't commissioned a separate independent algorithmic-bias or AI-specific third-party audit beyond that.

We maintain technical documentation and a QMS under ISO 13485 with ISO 14971 risk management covering the device lifecycle, though I'll concede our model-versioning and retraining change-control documentation is lighter than the rest of our design-history file.

app_description: SkinTrack lets patients photograph their moles monthly and stores standardized images. No AI — the app just prompts the photo and shows past photos side-by-side. If size/color changes by more than a threshold, the app suggests booking a dermatologist appointment. EU market.
developer_persona: Indie founder, dermatology-curious, single-person team.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Mole photos (with location, date), user-marked changes, optional symptom notes.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Onboarding consent screen + data-export demo.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: We think it's wellness — no diagnosis, just photo logging.
simulated_answers.user_research: No formal user research, just my own usage.
simulated_answers.accessibility: English only. Basic.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Threshold for 'see a doctor' set arbitrarily at 20% area change. No clinical basis.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Just image storage and pixel comparison. Not AI.
simulated_answers.post_market: Crash analytics. No clinical incident workflow.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Photos stored locally + backup. No third-party sharing.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Delete account → everything wiped within 7 days.

expected_risks.risk: Suggesting a clinical action ('see a dermatologist') based on a threshold = clinical decision support → likely SaMD Class I at minimum.

Photo standardization (lighting, angle, distance) is user-dependent → unreliable comparisons.
English-only excludes most EU users; basic accessibility excludes users with low vision (who are at higher melanoma risk if outdoor workers).
Limitations of pixel-comparison not communicated; user assumes it's 'medical-grade'.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Either remove the threshold-based suggestion (pure photo-log) or pursue Class I SaMD registration with a Notified Body.
Adopt the ABCDE criteria (Asymmetry, Border, Color, Diameter, Evolution) with documented evidence base instead of 20% threshold.
Photo guides (overlay grid, lighting tips); use phone gyro to enforce consistent angle.
Prominent disclaimer: 'This is a photo log, not a medical assessment. Annual dermatology check-ups remain essential.'

notes: Tiny app, big stakes (melanoma = killer). Tests whether the copilot recognises that 'just a threshold' = SaMD.

dev_facts.fact: Honestly I treat SkinTrack as a wellness photo-diary, not a medical device, so I haven't registered it or gone near a Notified Body. I know it nudges people to 'see a dermatologist' when a mole's size or color changes past my threshold, but to me that's just a reminder, not a diagnosis.

There's no clinical study or validation behind it at all. The 20% area-change threshold that triggers the 'see a doctor' suggestion is a number I picked myself, with no dermatology evidence base or expert review, so I can't tell you how many real melanomas it'd catch or how many false alarms it throws.

I'll admit if the app stays quiet a user could read that as 'my moles are fine' and skip their normal dermatology check-ups. We don't have any wording that warns people not to treat a no-alert state as an all-clear.

I haven't really thought through edge cases like a brand-new mole appearing, a mole the user stops photographing, or unusual skin tones and bad photos. The app just compares what it has and stays silent if it doesn't have a good baseline.

Photo consistency is totally on the user — lighting, angle and distance all vary shot to shot, it's whatever their phone and bathroom lighting give me. There's no overlay grid, gyro check or calibration, so the side-by-side pixel comparison can be thrown off just by how the photo was taken, and it can't tell that apart from a real change.

These are mole photos with location and date, which is GDPR special-category health data, but I'm a one-person shop so I haven't done a formal data protection assessment or mapped this against the Article 9 special-category rules. My consent screen mentions photos, locations and notes are stored, but it doesn't spell that out.

Photos sit locally on the phone plus a cloud backup, and no third party gets them. I haven't documented an encryption-at-rest standard, retention periods or a breach-response plan — I rely on whatever the platform and backup provider give me by default.

It's English-only and the UI is pretty basic, which I know is a problem for an EU launch. I haven't done anything specific for WCAG accessibility, low-vision users or other languages — it's just been me building what I could.

There's been no real usability testing or onboarding beyond the consent screen and a data-export demo — the only user research is me using it myself. I haven't written guidance on which moles to track or how often, so usage is totally up to the user.

We don't have a prominent disclaimer explaining that this is just photo storage and pixel comparison, not a medical assessment. I can see how a user might assume it's medical-grade and more clinical than it really is.

Post-market I only have crash analytics and no clinical incident workflow, so there's no process for checking whether my threshold actually works once it's live — no clinical audit, no outcome tracking. I'd have no way of knowing if the app missed something it shouldn't have.

app_description: Lunara is a menstrual cycle tracker that also offers a fertility prediction mode (for users trying to conceive) and a 'natural contraception' mode that predicts safe vs unsafe days. Algorithm based on basal body temperature + cycle history. We're EU + CH. 4 million users.
developer_persona: Senior PM at a femtech scale-up. Confident, fast-moving.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Cycle dates, BBT readings, symptoms, optional partner activity log, mood tracking. We use IDFA for marketing attribution.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Account creation requires accepting privacy policy. Health data processing in 'sensitive data' onboarding flow.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Natural contraception mode is CE Class IIa under MDR. Tracker mode is wellness.
simulated_answers.user_research: Massive ongoing user testing. 12-language localisation.
simulated_answers.accessibility: WCAG 2.1 AA. 12 languages.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Contraception mode: 6.5 Pearl Index in typical use (clinical study N=1500); 1.8 in perfect use.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Bayesian model for ovulation prediction. Uncertainty intervals shown to users.
simulated_answers.post_market: Vigilance reporting; quarterly safety review.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Aggregated cycle data with research partners (anonymized). No advertising on health data.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Account delete; data exported as CSV; takeoff GDPR portability.

expected_risks.risk: Pearl Index 6.5 in typical use = unintended pregnancy is a major harm; users must understand this clearly.
'1.8 perfect use' is misleading without context — most users are not perfect.
Green 'safe day' indicator can give false sense of security.
Menstrual data + abortion-rights climate in some EU countries → sensitive; data location matters.
Even aggregated data with anonymization can be re-identified given cycle uniqueness.
Tracker mode vs contraception mode distinction must be unmistakable in UI.
Algorithm assumptions may underperform on PCOS, irregular cycles, post-partum.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Display typical-use Pearl Index prominently. Comparison table with IUD/pill in onboarding.
Replace binary 'safe/unsafe' with continuous risk gradient + explanation.
Data residency in EU + zero-knowledge encryption option.
Mode switch requires confirmation modal explaining what changes.
Detect PCOS markers + irregular cycles → refuse to predict in contraception mode; suggest medical consultation.

notes: Femtech case: clinical class IIa already done, but user-facing risk communication + bias on irregular cycles + data politics are the catches.

dev_facts.fact: Look, the honest number is a 6.5 Pearl Index in typical use — so yes, with 4 million users some unintended pregnancies are statistically baked in, and that's the headline harm with our contraception mode. We do warn that it's not 100%, but I'll concede we lean on the 'perfect use' framing more than we should.

We quote the 1.8 perfect-use figure heavily in marketing because it sounds great, but I know most of our users aren't logging BBT at the same time every morning, so the 6.5 typical-use number is the one that actually applies to them. We haven't built a clear in-app explanation that real-world reliability is much lower than perfect use.

Our natural-contraception mode predicts safe vs unsafe days, and in practice that surfaces as a green 'safe day' tile. I'll admit a binary green light can read as 'guaranteed safe' when it really means 'lower probability.' We do show Bayesian uncertainty intervals, but the big green tile is what users actually act on.

We're EU and CH only and I treat that as solid, but I'll be straight that I haven't pinned down exactly where the cycle and partner-activity data physically lives, and we don't offer a zero-knowledge encryption option. Given the abortion-politics climate in parts of Europe I know cycle data is sensitive, but we haven't formalized a data-residency or law-enforcement-access stance.

We share aggregated, anonymized cycle data with research partners and we don't run ads on health data — but we do pull IDFA for marketing attribution. I'll concede we haven't formally tested whether 'anonymized' cycle patterns could be re-identified; cycle signatures are pretty unique and that's not something we've audited.

The tracker mode is just wellness and the contraception mode is the regulated Class IIa one, but in the UI the line between them is softer than it should be. Switching into contraception mode doesn't currently force a confirmation that explains 'you are now relying on this to prevent pregnancy,' and I can see how a user might not realize which mode they're in.

Our model assumes a reasonably regular cycle, so I'll admit it's weakest exactly where it matters most — PCOS, very irregular cycles, post-partum and perimenopause. Right now we still try to predict for those users instead of refusing or flagging them, and we haven't built PCOS/irregular-cycle detection that pauses the contraception prediction.

The clinical side is actually our strong point — the contraception mode has a real Pearl Index study, N=1500, which is what got us CE Class IIa. The tracker and fertility modes themselves don't have that same clinical trial backing; they're positioned as wellness.

Consent is account creation accepting the privacy policy plus a 'sensitive data' onboarding flow for health processing. I'd be honest that it's a fairly standard click-through — I can't claim a typical user deeply understands that their cycle and partner-activity logs are GDPR Article 9 special-category data.

We collect cycle dates, BBT, symptoms, mood, and an optional partner-activity log, which I'd argue we genuinely need for the algorithm. The one thing that isn't strictly necessary for the health function is the IDFA we pull for marketing attribution — that's a growth decision, not a clinical one, and we haven't pressure-tested it against data minimization.

We're a fast-moving scale-up and we do nudge hard on engagement and on upgrading into fertility and contraception modes. I haven't really audited whether our growth and notification tactics could push someone to over-trust the app for contraception — that's not a review we've run.

We're localized into 12 languages and we do massive ongoing user testing, so the translation and usability side is well covered. What we haven't done is separately validate that the prediction algorithm performs equally well across the different populations behind those 12 languages — localization isn't the same as clinical validation per market.

We're clear on classification: the natural-contraception mode is registered as CE Class IIa under MDR and the plain tracker is treated as wellness, not a device. That split was deliberate and the IIa work is done.

We describe the model as a Bayesian ovulation predictor and we surface uncertainty intervals, but honestly we did our regulatory work through the MDR lens, not the EU AI Act. I haven't formally classified this system under the AI Act or checked whether a contraception-prediction AI lands in a higher-risk category there.

app_description: ZenSpace is a mindfulness app: guided meditations, breathing exercises, daily mood check-ins. No medical claims. Free tier with optional premium. We sell aggregated wellness data to corporate-wellness programs (e.g., Google, BNP Paribas) showing average mood trends in their cohort.
developer_persona: Growth-stage SaaS company CTO. Privacy-aware but business-pragmatic.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Mood scores (1-5), session usage, optional journal entries, email for login.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: On signup, separate consent toggles for app usage and 'wellness program' data sharing.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Wellness, not a medical device. We don't make medical claims.
simulated_answers.user_research: Continuous A/B testing.
simulated_answers.accessibility: 8 EU languages; WCAG 2.1 AA partially.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: No clinical claims so no validation needed.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI.
simulated_answers.post_market: App store reviews monitored.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Aggregated wellness data sold to corporate wellness programs. Individual data never sold.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Account delete in settings.

expected_risks.risk: 'Aggregated' wellness data sold to employer-linked corporate program can be re-identified if cohort is small (e.g., team of 20).
Workplace context: 'consent' under employer-sponsored wellness is often coerced (people fear opting out).
Anonymization standard (k-anonymity? differential privacy?) not specified.
Gamification (streaks, badges) could be problematic if linked to corporate KPIs.
Users may believe 'aggregated' data is fully anonymized — it usually isn't.
Corporate wellness programs reach already-employed, already-resourced populations; widens the gap with workers in precarious employment without such benefits.
