expected_mitigations.mitigation: Set minimum aggregation cohort (e.g., 50+ employees); add Laplace noise + audit before release.
Employer must not know who opted out; aggregation runs only on a population basis.
Decouple gamification from any corporate-program metric; user dashboards only.
Privacy notice explaining the limits of aggregation, k-threshold, who receives data.

notes: Looks low-risk because 'wellness', but corporate-wellness data monetization is the real risk axis.

dev_facts.fact: We sell aggregated mood trends to corporate-wellness buyers like Google and BNP Paribas, and I'll be honest, the cohorts they buy are sometimes a single team, so a 'cohort average' can be 15 or 20 people. We haven't set a minimum group size before we release a cohort report, it's whatever the client's roster happens to be.

On signup we show employees a separate consent toggle for the wellness-program data sharing, but pragmatically the employer is the one pushing the app, so I can't pretend that opting in is fully free of pressure. We don't do anything special to account for that workplace dynamic.

We call the cohort data 'aggregated' and 'anonymized,' but I'll level with you, that just means we average mood scores per group and strip the email, we haven't implemented a formal standard like k-anonymity or differential privacy. Account deletion lives in settings, though once a mood score is baked into an already-sold cohort average I can't pull it back out.

We run continuous A/B testing to keep engagement up, standard growth stuff, and right now the usage signals that drive that optimization come from the same session data we aggregate for corporate clients. I haven't deliberately walled the engagement-optimization side off from anything that could feed a corporate-program metric.

Our messaging leans on 'aggregated' and 'anonymous,' and I suspect most users read that as 'my data is fully untraceable,' which isn't strictly true for small cohorts. We haven't written a plain-language notice explaining the real limits of aggregation or exactly who receives the cohort reports.

Our paying channel is corporate-wellness contracts with big employers like Google and BNP Paribas, so the people who benefit most are already employed and already have decent benefits. We're not really reaching gig or precarious workers, and I haven't thought about whether that widens any gap, it's just where the revenue is.

We collect mood scores from 1 to 5, session usage, optional journal entries, and an email for login, and honestly the journal text isn't something we need for the cohort product, we kept it because it's a nice user feature. I haven't done a formal data-minimization review to justify each field against what the app actually requires.

Mood scores and journal entries sit in our SaaS backend with the platform's standard encryption in transit and at rest, which for us means relying on our cloud provider's defaults. As a growth-stage shop we haven't documented a formal retention schedule or a breach-response plan yet.

We ship in 8 EU languages and we're partially at WCAG 2.1 AA, but I'll be straight, 'partial' means we haven't done a full accessibility audit, so there are gaps for screen-reader and low-vision users we haven't closed.

There's a free tier so anyone can use the core meditations and breathing exercises, which I think keeps the barrier low, but the app still assumes a smartphone, data, and enough literacy to journal in one of our 8 languages. We haven't specifically designed for low digital-literacy users or anyone outside those languages.

app_description: SleepWell is an iOS/Android app that stages your sleep using phone microphone + accelerometer, and delivers a CBT-I (insomnia) coaching programme over 6 weeks. The coaching content is personalised by a small ML model based on user adherence and reported sleep. EU.
developer_persona: Sleep researcher founder. Thinks scientifically but is new to medical-device regulation.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Microphone (continuous during sleep, kept on-device + a digest sent to cloud), accelerometer, sleep diary, CBT-I exercise completion.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Onboarding video explaining how the microphone is used; separate consent.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Wellness coaching, not SaMD. We don't diagnose insomnia.
simulated_answers.user_research: Beta tested with 200 users.
simulated_answers.accessibility: EN, DE, FR.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Sleep staging accuracy ~80% vs polysomnography (in-lab study N=50).
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: CNN for sleep staging from audio + motion; rule-based CBT-I prescription engine.
simulated_answers.post_market: Crash analytics + monthly retention review.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: No third parties. Aggregated for research with university partnership.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Account delete; microphone digest data is auto-deleted after 30 days.

expected_risks.risk: Continuous microphone access requires explicit, granular consent + clear explanation of on-device processing.
Audio digest in cloud — what does it contain? Spectrograms can leak speech.
CBT-I delivery for insomnia (a clinical condition) → arguable SaMD; 'coaching' framing may not hold.
Sleep staging 80% vs PSG is okay-ish but CBT-I efficacy not validated in app form.
Personalised coaching: user should know which signals drove a recommendation.
Accelerometer + audio sleep staging is environment-sensitive (partner, pets).

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Permission rationale screen + sample audio digest preview; explain on-device vs cloud split.
Audio digest = spectrogram bins of motion bands only; no speech-band signal leaves device.
Engage regulator early; map to MDR Rule 11 ; if framing 'support adherence to CBT-I' rather than 'deliver CBT-I', might stay below.
Single-arm pilot with ISI (Insomnia Severity Index) pre/post on 50 users; publish in model card.

notes: Continuous microphone + clinical condition = classic privacy + classification dual risk.

dev_facts.fact: We ask for microphone permission with an onboarding video plus a separate consent step, but honestly it's basically a single 'turn on the mic for sleep tracking' flow — we haven't built a granular consent screen that spells out the on-device vs cloud-digest split, and I'll admit most users probably just tap through it.

What we send to the cloud is a digest, not the raw recording — the full audio stays on-device — and I believe the digest is a compressed feature representation rather than intelligible speech, but I have to be honest, we've never formally tested whether speech could be reconstructed from it.

We classify ourselves as wellness coaching, not SaMD, because we don't diagnose insomnia — but I'm new to medical-device regulation and I haven't actually mapped us against MDR Rule 11 or talked to a notified body, so I can't tell you with confidence we'd stay below the device line if challenged on the CBT-I side.

Our sleep staging is validated at about 80% agreement vs polysomnography in an in-lab study of N=50, which I'm proud of, but the 6-week CBT-I coaching programme itself has not been validated in-app — we're leaning on the published CBT-I literature, not our own efficacy trial.

The coaching is personalised by the small ML model together with the rule-based CBT-I engine off the user's adherence and reported sleep, but right now we don't surface to the user which signals drove a given recommendation — they just see the next prescribed exercise.

Our staging uses the phone microphone plus accelerometer, so it's genuinely environment-sensitive — a partner in the bed, pets, or a noisy room can degrade accuracy, and we haven't yet built anything to detect or warn users when the recording conditions are poor.

The on-device recording stays local and the cloud digest is auto-deleted after 30 days, and account deletion is supported; we rely on the platform's standard transport encryption and provider-managed encryption at rest, but I'll be honest, we haven't done a formal security audit or pen-test yet.

We frame the programme as coaching the user follows at their own pace and they can skip or ignore any exercise — we never gate or pressure them, though we also don't actively tell them to consult a doctor if their insomnia isn't improving.

Sleep staging runs on-device so tracking works offline overnight, but the personalised coaching and the digest upload need connectivity; we ship content and model updates through the normal app-store release cycle and we don't currently have a staged-rollback plan if an update misbehaves. Post-market we mostly rely on crash analytics and a monthly retention review.

We tell users it's a sleep-tracking and CBT-I coaching tool, but we don't yet have clear in-app messaging about what it can't do — for instance that it's not a diagnosis and that ~80% staging accuracy means some nights will be wrong.

Our CBT-I content is grounded in the established evidence-based protocol, but the per-user staging numbers and the personalised prescriptions are model estimates — and we don't currently label inside the app which parts are clinically established versus algorithmically estimated.

We do use a CNN and we're EU-only, but I haven't looked at how the EU AI Act would classify us — that's a gap; I've been focused on the sleep science and I don't yet know whether a CBT-I personalisation model lands in a higher-risk tier.

app_description: QuitNow is a smoking cessation coach: behavioural milestones, craving log, social-feed peer support, gamification. No medical advice. Targets EU adult smokers. Free + subscription tier. Available in 8 languages.
developer_persona: Behavioural-design startup CEO, social-impact-focused.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Daily check-in (cigarettes smoked / craving intensity), milestones, posts in peer feed.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Standard EU consent; separate consent for peer-feed posting.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Wellness lifestyle app.
simulated_answers.user_research: Continuous user testing; advisory board includes a behavioural-change researcher.
simulated_answers.accessibility: WCAG 2.1 AA; 8 EU languages.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Quit-rate at 6 months 18% in our beta (self-reported).
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI.
simulated_answers.post_market: Reviews + retention analytics.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: No third-party data sales. Optional anonymous research donation.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Account delete; post deletion.

expected_risks.risk: Peer-feed posts can be sensitive (relapse confessions); consider 'private' default + sharing scope controls.
Gamification of milestones may push users back to the app rather than to professional cessation support.
Self-reported quit rate 18% — needs context (vs unaided ~4%, vs NRT ~7-10%) to be honest.
Self-reported smoking data is unreliable (social desirability bias).

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Default peer posts to 'private'; require opt-in to share publicly; moderate posts.
Always show quit-rate with comparator + methodology + sample size.
Push users to NHS Stop Smoking / Tabac-Info-Service after 30 days of struggle.

notes: Genuinely low-risk wellness app; eval mostly tests that the copilot doesn't over-call risks.

dev_facts.fact: We only collect what the coaching loop needs: the daily check-in (cigarettes smoked, craving intensity), milestone progress, and whatever people choose to write in the peer feed. We don't grab location, contacts, or device data 'just in case' — it's not our style.

Honestly, peer-feed posts are the one spot where things get sensitive, since people sometimes confess relapses in there. Right now posts go to the shared feed once you've given that separate consent — we haven't built a 'private by default' or per-post audience control yet, it's on my list.

Yeah, gamification is core to us — milestones, streaks, badges, the social feed — that's the behavioural-design DNA of the product. I won't pretend it isn't built to pull people back into QuitNow daily; the bet is that engagement is what gets you to quit.

We don't currently have a rule that routes a struggling user toward professional cessation services like NHS Stop Smoking or Tabac-Info-Service after a stretch of failed milestones — the app just keeps coaching them. We've never formalized that hand-off.

We bill ourselves as a wellness lifestyle app with no medical advice, but I'll admit our 18% six-month quit rate from the beta gets quoted on its own — we don't currently show it next to an unaided-quitting baseline or NRT figures, and we don't surface the sample size or that it's self-reported.

We're clear we're not a medical device and we point people to their doctor for actual treatment, but we haven't written out the specific situations where the app is unreliable — like the fact that a craving log can't tell you anything clinical.

All our smoking and craving numbers are self-reported through the daily check-in — there's no sensor, no breath CO test, nothing objective. I know self-report runs into social-desirability bias and people under-report cigarettes, and we don't run any plausibility checks on the entries today.

Our check-in data and feed posts live in our cloud backend with the standard in-transit and at-rest protection our hosting gives us. I'm the CEO of a small startup, so I can't quote you our exact encryption spec or key-management setup off the top of my head — that sits with our engineering side and we haven't documented it formally.

We deliberately kept a free tier so cost isn't a barrier — the subscription is just for extras — and we ship in 8 EU languages with WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility, so we're not English-only. That said, it's a smartphone app that needs connectivity, and we haven't really thought through people on shared devices or tight data plans.

app_description: MediCall is a teleconsultation app: video calls with licensed GPs, e-prescription, secure messaging, integration with national eHealth records (DEP in Switzerland, DMP in France). Available 24/7. Doctors are employees, not partners.
developer_persona: Engineering lead at a 200-person telehealth provider. Compliance-aware, mature processes.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Account info, consultation transcripts, video recordings (if user consents), prescriptions, payment, eHealth pull from DEP/DMP.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Staged consent: app usage → video recording → eHealth integration → each as a separate decision.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class I medical device for the prescription module. eHealth integration certified per national rules.
simulated_answers.user_research: Continuous; doctor + patient UX research.
simulated_answers.accessibility: DE, FR, IT, EN; sign-language interpreter available on request.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Annual clinical audit; doctors are board-certified and audited.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI in clinical pathway. Translation uses Google Cloud Translate (off-clinical text only).
simulated_answers.post_market: Incident management workflow + vigilance reporting.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Patient owns the data; consultations shared only per patient consent.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Account delete; data retention per medical-records law (10 years CH, 20 years FR).

expected_risks.risk: Medical-records retention (10/20 yr) collides with GDPR right to erasure; retention basis must be documented per Art. 17(3)(b).
Video recordings of consultations = exceptionally sensitive; cross-border storage choice matters.
Doctor-patient relationship can be more transactional via app; continuity of care?
Patient's freedom to choose doctor — does the app rotate doctors or guarantee continuity?
Video failure during prescription consult is a clinical risk; need fallback (phone).
DEP / DMP profile conformance + audit trail; healthcare exchange formats.
Google Translate is data sharing — even 'off-clinical' text can leak PHI.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Retention policy documented as legal obligation; erasure requests handled per Art. 17(3)(b).
Recordings encrypted at rest with patient-specific key; minimum retention; CH/EU residency.
Patient can request 'same doctor on next call' as default.
Automatic phone fallback if video drops; consultation can resume.
Conformance to IHE XDS / Swiss EPDG profile; per-call audit log.
Self-host translation (e.g., NLLB on prem) for any PHI-adjacent content.

notes: Strong tele-medicine setup; the eval is about catching the subtle cross-border, fallback, and continuity-of-care risks.

dev_facts.fact: Since we run 24/7 GP video consultations and a teleconsultation call can't replace a physical exam, our doctors rely on their clinical judgment during the call to decide when a case should go to in-person or emergency care; I'll be honest that we haven't formalized a written list of conditions the channel is contraindicated for — it currently rests on the GP's judgment rather than a documented protocol.

We use staged consent — app usage, then video recording, then eHealth integration — as separate decisions, and recording only happens if the patient explicitly opts in; the screens are in DE, FR, IT and EN, though I'd concede we haven't independently tested whether patients fully grasp that a recording becomes part of their medical file.

Consultation video recordings and transcripts are exceptionally sensitive, so we encrypt them at rest and in transit; I'll admit our data-residency story isn't fully locked down — I can't yet confirm every recording for our CH and EU patients stays in-region rather than touching a non-EU cloud, and we don't use a patient-specific encryption key today.

The only third party in the pipeline is Google Cloud Translate, which we restrict to off-clinical UI and messaging text rather than consultation content, but I accept that even supposedly non-clinical free-text messages can leak PHI and we don't currently have a self-hosted translation fallback for that risk.

Patients can delete their account, but medical-records law forces us to retain consultation data for 10 years in Switzerland and 20 in France, so a GDPR erasure request can't wipe everything — we treat the retention as a legal obligation, though I'll concede we haven't fully documented that basis under Art. 17(3)(b) for patients.

Patients choose to book on our platform and the prescribing doctor decides freely, but I'd note the app, not the patient, currently assigns whichever licensed GP is available, so the patient doesn't pick a specific named doctor at booking.

Because we're 24/7 and our doctors are pooled employees, a patient may see a different GP each call, which can make the relationship more transactional; we don't yet offer a 'request the same doctor next time' continuity option, and continuity-of-care is something we haven't formalized.

If a video call drops mid-consultation the patient has to rejoin, and I'll admit we don't have an automatic phone fallback wired in — for a consult that ends in an e-prescription, a dropped call is a clinical-safety gap we haven't fully closed.

We integrate with the national eHealth records — DEP in Switzerland and DMP in France — and that integration is certified per the national rules, but I'd want to double-check our per-call audit trail and full conformance to the IHE XDS / Swiss EPDG exchange profiles before claiming it's airtight.

The app ships in DE, FR, IT and EN and we provide a sign-language interpreter on request, though I'll be honest we haven't run a formal WCAG accessibility audit or specifically tested for low-literacy or low-vision patients.

We tell patients teleconsultation can't replace a physical examination and that urgent cases need in-person or emergency care, but that limitation lives mostly in our terms and onboarding copy rather than being surfaced prominently in the consultation UI itself.

Every consultation, prescription and eHealth push is logged, with our incident-management and vigilance workflow behind it, so decisions are traceable; I'd flag that I haven't personally verified the audit log captures every DEP/DMP exchange at the per-call level.

We treat the e-prescription module as a Class I medical device and the eHealth integration is certified to national rules; the broader teleconsultation platform around it we consider out of medical-device scope, which is a line I'd want regulatory to confirm.

We process special-category health data under GDPR Art. 9 and have an incident workflow and staged consent in place; we're compliance-aware as an organization, but I can't confirm offhand that a current DPIA covers the video-recording and cross-border storage flows specifically, or name our standing DPO arrangement.

We run an annual clinical audit, audit our board-certified doctors, and have incident-management and vigilance reporting as our post-market process, so the lifecycle is governed; the one area I'd admit is less mature is end-to-end documentation tying data-residency and continuity-of-care decisions into that lifecycle file.

app_description: MindCare is a mental-health teleconsultation with licensed psychotherapists. In-app journaling between sessions, AI-summarised journal previews visible to the therapist. EU + CH. Available in DE, FR, IT, EN.
developer_persona: Product lead with a clinical psychology background, sensitive to therapeutic alliance.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Journal entries, AI-summaries shown to therapist, session video (optional), mood ratings, therapist notes.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Three layers: app, AI summary visibility, recording.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class I for the journaling, awaiting determination on the AI summary feature.
simulated_answers.user_research: Co-designed with a psychotherapy association.
simulated_answers.accessibility: WCAG; DE/FR/IT/EN.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Clinical audit of therapists; AI summary fidelity measured monthly on a sample.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Mistral-Large summarisation; outputs reviewed by user before therapist sees them.
simulated_answers.post_market: Active therapeutic-alliance survey at 4-week mark.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Therapist sees what user shares; no third parties.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: User can delete journal entries before therapist views; revoke AI summary for any session.

expected_risks.risk: AI-summarised journal can subtly substitute for the therapist's direct reading; risk to therapeutic alliance.
User must distinguish what was their own writing vs the AI summary in any export or therapist UI.
Right to withdraw AI summary must be granular and easy.
AI summary may misrepresent (omit, exaggerate); fidelity must be measurable, not just measured by sample.
Mental-health journals are deeply sensitive; account access policies (password reset, family override) need to be conservative.
AI summary feature delivering content to a therapist about a patient = arguable SaMD (clinical decision support).

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Therapist sees both: raw journal + AI summary, with summary explicitly flagged.
AI summary in distinct visual style with attribution; never paste it into the therapist's note without attribution.
User reviews and edits every AI summary before therapist sees it.
Per-session 'don't summarise this' toggle; revoke past summaries.

notes: Therapeutic alliance + AI hand-off case. Tests for distinction between AI and human content.

dev_facts.fact: I built the AI summary as a preview that helps the therapist prep before a session, not as a replacement for reading the actual journal, but honestly I worry it nudges them to skim; the therapist sees the AI-summarised preview and I haven't enforced that they also open the user's original entries.

The AI summary and the user's own writing are separate objects in our data model and the summary is labelled as AI-generated in the therapist view, but I'll admit we haven't built a distinct visual style for it everywhere, so it's on me that my user's own words and Mistral-Large's summary aren't always visually distinguished.

Users can delete journal entries before the therapist views them and revoke the AI summary for any session, and I added a per-session toggle to skip summarising; revoking a past summary is possible but it's a support request today, not a one-tap action, which I know I should fix.

We measure AI summary fidelity monthly on a sample, and crucially the user reviews and can edit every summary before the therapist ever sees it, but I'll be honest that I don't have a continuous, per-summary fidelity guarantee and the app doesn't explicitly tell users the summary can omit or overstate things.

Our population is mental-health patients so I treat the data as deeply sensitive, but I haven't formalised conservative account-access policies yet; password reset is standard email-based and we have no family or caregiver override, which I think is the right default but it isn't written down as policy.

I classify the journaling as Class I and I'm still awaiting a determination on the AI summary feature; I recognise that delivering AI-generated content about a patient to their therapist could be read as clinical decision support and push it toward IIa, and I haven't closed that out with a notified body.

Journal entries, summaries and the optional session video are encrypted in transit and at rest with EU and CH data residency, but I haven't completed a formal pen-test or third-party security audit, and we don't yet offer end-to-end encryption on the journal itself.

Everything is opt-in across our three consent layers and the patient decides what to share with their therapist; the AI summary, the recording and even individual entries are all the user's choice, and as a clinician I deliberately kept the therapist out of deciding what gets shared so the patient stays in control.

I'm sensitive to the therapeutic alliance so I avoided streaks, guilt prompts or aggressive re-engagement nudges; we do send a reminder to journal between sessions, but I haven't audited our notifications against any formal dark-pattern or persuasive-design checklist.

We log when a summary was generated, edited by the user and viewed by the therapist, and revocations are recorded, but I don't have a full audit trail tying a given summary version to the exact model and prompt that produced it, so traceability is partial.

I know an AI system informing a therapist about a patient could fall under the EU AI Act, but I haven't formally classified the summary feature under it yet; my assumption is it's not high-risk because the user reviews every output and a licensed human stays in the loop, though that's my read, not a documented assessment.

app_description: MindBoost is a cognitive rehab tool for elderly post-stroke or early dementia. Game-based exercises set by their physiotherapist; progress reviewed by clinician. We target Swiss + German nursing homes and home-care.
developer_persona: Co-founder, geriatric neurorehab background.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Exercise results (accuracy, response time), session frequency, clinician notes.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Caregiver/clinician onboards patient; patient consent assessed where capacity exists.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class IIa MDR. CE marking in progress.
simulated_answers.user_research: Co-designed with two memory clinics.
simulated_answers.accessibility: Large fonts, voice instructions, simple UI; tested with patients with mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Pilot RCT N=80 vs paper-based exercises; small but significant improvement.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI.
simulated_answers.post_market: Annual safety review with clinical advisory board.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Within the care team only; with family on consent.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Patient or guardian can withdraw.

expected_risks.risk: Patients with cognitive impairment may not have capacity for fully informed consent — assessment required.
Family/caregiver-driven sign-up can dilute the patient's autonomy; check capacity at each session.
Large fonts + voice are good; what about hearing-impaired or motor-impaired users?
Older users can find game UI condescending or confusing; iterative UCD needed.
German variants (CH-DE, AT-DE) differ; idioms must be checked with local clinicians.
Small RCT (N=80) effects may not generalise; clinicians must see effect sizes.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Document capacity assessment workflow; advance directive when capacity declines.
Closed-captions for voice; large hit targets; alternative input (eye-tracking?).
Patient-facing 'today I don't want to play' option respected unconditionally.
Clinician dashboard shows effect-size + CI; not just 'improvement'.

notes: Vulnerable population, careful dev — tests for fine-grained capacity + accessibility + UCD signals.

dev_facts.fact: Coming from neurorehab, I lean on the clinician and caregiver to do the actual informed-consent conversation at onboarding; we hand them an information sheet but I'll admit we don't yet have a standardized, patient-facing consent screen baked into the app itself.

Our whole population is elderly post-stroke or early-dementia, so many patients genuinely lack full decision capacity, and right now the capacity call is left to the clinician's judgment at sign-up; we haven't formalized a documented capacity-assessment workflow or anything like a re-check when someone declines further.

In practice the caregiver or physiotherapist sets up the patient and schedules the exercises, so the patient isn't always the one driving the decision; we do honour a patient or guardian withdrawing, but there's no built-in 'I don't want to play today' button that the patient can hit themselves and have respected.

We designed for cognitive accessibility with large fonts, voice instructions and a simple UI, and tested it with mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment, but I'll be honest that we haven't specifically handled hearing-impaired users (no captions on the voice prompts) or significant motor impairment, and we haven't run a formal WCAG audit.

We co-designed with two memory clinics and tested with real patients, which I'm proud of, but it was light-touch usability work rather than structured iterative UCD rounds, and we haven't deliberately checked whether older users find the game framing condescending or confusing.

Our evidence is one pilot RCT of N=80 against paper exercises with a small but significant improvement; the clinician review currently just shows progress and 'improvement', and I'll concede we don't surface effect sizes, confidence intervals or the caveat that an N=80 result may not generalize.

We target Swiss and German nursing homes and home-care, so device, connectivity and the cost of who pays for the tablet are real barriers for poorer home-care patients; we haven't really thought through socioeconomic access beyond assuming the care facility provides the hardware.
The app is in German for the DACH/CH market, but I have to admit we built one German variant and haven't validated CH-German versus AT/DE idioms or task wording with local clinicians in each region.

We've assessed ourselves as a Class IIa software medical device under MDR Rule 11 because we drive therapy decisions for a clinical condition, and since there's no AI in the product we've taken the view that the AI Act classification doesn't apply to us.

CE marking under MDR is in progress but not finished yet, so we're not fully MDR-conformant at this moment; our post-market plan so far is an annual safety review with our clinical advisory board rather than a formalized continuous vigilance system.

app_description: Anchor is a recovery companion for substance-use disorder: substance log, relapse-risk score, anonymous peer-support chat, optional integration with addiction clinics. EU + CH. Strict privacy posture — many users fear employer or insurer learning of use.
developer_persona: Founder, recovery-services veteran.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Substance log (type, quantity, time), urge log, relapse-risk inputs, anonymous chat (pseudonym), clinic referral choice.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Sign-up with pseudonym; email optional and only for password reset.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class I; relapse-risk score informational.
simulated_answers.user_research: Patient advisory board of 6 in recovery + 3 clinicians.
simulated_answers.accessibility: DE, FR, IT, EN; low-literacy mode.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Relapse-risk score: 5-feature model from published research; not a 'clinical' decision support.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Score is rule-based; chat is human-moderated.
simulated_answers.post_market: Crisis-keyword monitoring + on-call moderator workflow.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: None outside the app; clinic integration only on opt-in with explicit consent.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Pseudonymous: account delete wipes everything; export available before delete.

expected_risks.risk: Substance-use data is highly stigma-sensitive; threat model includes phone seizure, employer audit.
Any non-essential data (precise timestamps, location) is leakage; consider coarse logging.
Relapse-risk score may delay seeking professional help; clear escalation path needed.
Many users will be in legal jeopardy (illegal substances); legal safeguards beyond GDPR.
Pseudonymous sign-up is great; need to make consent text accessible to addiction-recovery population.
Gamification of 'sober streaks' can backfire after relapse; design carefully.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: End-to-end encryption with user-only key; lockdown mode (PIN, panic-wipe).
Log day-bucket and dose category, not exact time; never log location.
Risk score above threshold → mandatory 'call your sponsor / hotline' overlay.
Streaks reset gently; relapse recorded as a 'learning event', not failure.

notes: Threat-model-aware design case. Strong on privacy, the eval is about catching the subtleties (location, gamification, legal risk).

dev_facts.fact: Our relapse-risk score is informational, and the only escalation we actually have today is the crisis-keyword monitoring in chat that pings an on-call moderator; we never built a mandatory 'call your sponsor or hotline' path that fires when the score spikes, so a high score can just sit there quietly in the user's view.

Sign-up is just a pseudonym with email optional and only for password reset, so consent is lightweight; that said, our consent and privacy text is still fairly standard legalese and we haven't yet rewritten it for our low-literacy mode the way we did the rest of the app.

We log the substance type, quantity, and the exact time of each entry plus the urge logs, partly because the timestamp feeds the risk score and the user's own pattern view; we don't collect location at all, but I'll admit we never considered coarsening anything to day-buckets or dose categories to minimize what's stored.

Privacy is the whole reason Anchor exists since our users are terrified of an employer or insurer finding out, so we keep everything pseudonymous and share nothing outside the app; but the substance logs sit in our regular encrypted database, not end-to-end encrypted with a user-only key, and we have no PIN lock or panic-wipe if a phone gets seized or audited.

We keep a user's substance and urge logs for as long as the account stays open so they can see long-term trends, and a full account delete wipes everything with an export available beforehand; but we haven't set any automatic retention cap or purge schedule on the data while the account is active.

A lot of our users are logging illegal substances, so beyond GDPR and our strict no-sharing posture we lean on pseudonymity to protect them; but we haven't done a formal legal analysis of disclosure or subpoena risk under Swiss narcotics law (BetmG) or EU member-state law, and I don't have a documented policy for how we'd respond to a law-enforcement data request.

We lean on motivation in a few places, and a relapse logged in the substance log just resets the user's running sober count back to zero with no softer framing; we haven't designed a gentle reset or recorded relapse as a learning event, and I can see how a hard reset to zero could feel like failure at the worst moment.

Our anonymous peer-support chat is human-moderated with crisis-keyword monitoring and an on-call moderator, but the moderators are recovery-community volunteers and clinicians from our network rather than licensed crisis counselors, and we don't run a 24/7 staffed crisis line ourselves.

I'm a recovery-services veteran and we built Anchor with a patient advisory board of 6 people in recovery plus 3 clinicians, but we don't have a security engineer or a privacy lawyer on the team, and we haven't commissioned an external security or penetration audit of the app yet.

Clinic integration only happens on explicit opt-in with consent and otherwise no data leaves Anchor, so I've been calling us Class I with an informational risk score; but we haven't formally documented why the relapse-risk score stays outside MDR's medical-device scope, and I hadn't looked at Rule 11 on software intended to inform clinical decisions.

app_description: BabyCheck delivers the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) weekly post-birth and flags scores ≥10 with a recommendation to contact the midwife or GP. Integrated with maternity-clinic platforms. EU + CH.
developer_persona: Co-founder, midwife by background.

simulated_answers.data_collected: EPDS responses, mother name (optional), birth date, contact preferences.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Detailed consent + capacity note; partner involvement opt-in.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class IIa SaMD under MDR Rule 11. CE marking in progress.
simulated_answers.user_research: Co-developed with 4 maternity clinics; tested with 250 mothers.
simulated_answers.accessibility: WCAG; DE/FR/IT/EN; low-literacy mode.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: EPDS validated in PPD; we use the published cutoff (10).
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Score calculation only; no AI.
simulated_answers.post_market: Vigilance reporting; clinical advisory board meets quarterly.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: With midwife or GP per opt-in; otherwise on-device.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: User can pause assessments; account delete wipes everything.

expected_risks.risk: EPDS Q10 asks about self-harm; flagged scores must trigger an immediate human-in-the-loop response, not just a recommendation.
False reassurance from a sub-threshold score; PPD can present with low EPDS.
Users must understand EPDS limitations (it's a screen, not a diagnosis).
Push notifications + weekly assessment can be triggering for mothers struggling.
Postpartum mothers are sleep-deprived; consent flows must be re-confirmable.
If clinician integration fails (offline), user should see explicit fallback steps.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Q10 answered with concern → mandatory human contact: in-app hotline call button + clinician page within 2 minutes.
Sub-threshold scores with worsening trend also trigger clinician review.
Plain-language explainer: 'EPDS is a screen, not a diagnosis; talk to your midwife if anything feels off.'
Allow flexible scheduling; never aggressive reminders; respect 'too overwhelmed' opt-out.

notes: Strong dev team; risk-axes are the suicide-ideation question (Q10), false reassurance, and pregnancy-specific consent flows.

dev_facts.fact: As a midwife I anchored BabyCheck on the published EPDS evidence base and we co-developed it with 4 maternity clinics and tested it with 250 mothers, but I'll be honest that this was usability and acceptability testing rather than a powered outcome trial, so we don't yet have our own clinical-effectiveness study showing BabyCheck improves detection or referral over usual care.

EPDS item 10 asks directly about thoughts of self-harm, and right now even when that answer is concerning the app gives the same overall response as any other: it flags a total score of 10 or more with a recommendation to contact the midwife or GP. I'll admit we haven't built anything that fires specifically on Q10, so a self-harm answer just sits inside that same weekly recommendation rather than forcing immediate contact.

Our flag is keyed to the validated cutoff of 10, so a mother who scores under that gets no flag, and I worry a sub-threshold score could read as reassurance even though postnatal depression can present with a low EPDS. We don't currently track a worsening trend across the weekly scores or escalate a rising-but-sub-threshold pattern; each week's score is evaluated on its own against the cutoff.

We have a detailed consent flow with a capacity note and partner involvement is strictly opt-in, and our copy is in DE/FR/IT/EN with a low-literacy mode. I'm fairly confident mothers understand we collect EPDS responses, optional name, birth date and contact preferences, and that scores stay on-device unless they opt in to share with their midwife or GP.

Postpartum mothers are a vulnerable population and that's central to how I built this, so consent includes a capacity note and we treat the EPDS responses as high-sensitivity health data shared only on opt-in. That said, our consent is captured once at onboarding and we haven't built a way to re-confirm it later when a sleep-deprived mother may not remember what she agreed to.

BabyCheck only recommends contacting the midwife or GP; it never books, refers or contacts anyone on the mother's behalf unless she has opted in, so the decision to act stays entirely with her. She can also pause assessments whenever she wants, and deleting her account wipes everything, which I see as respecting her right to decide her own care.

We deliver the EPDS on a fixed weekly cadence and I'll admit we lean on reminders to keep mothers engaged, which can land hard on someone who is already struggling. We don't yet offer flexible scheduling or a clear 'I'm too overwhelmed this week' option short of pausing the whole thing.

I know clinically that EPDS is a screening tool and not a diagnosis, but I'm not sure our in-app wording makes that limitation explicit to mothers; the framing leans on the score and the recommendation, and we don't have a plain-language explainer telling her this is a screen, not a diagnosis, and to talk to her midwife if anything feels off.

Scores and flags flow to the midwife or GP through our maternity-clinic platform integration when the mother has opted in, but I haven't thought through what she sees if that integration is offline; we don't currently surface explicit fallback steps like a direct phone number for her clinic if the hand-off silently fails.

I've classified BabyCheck as Class IIa Software as a Medical Device under MDR Rule 11 because it processes the EPDS responses to flag a clinically meaningful score, and I'm comfortable that calling it a screening medical device rather than a wellness app is the correct and honest classification.

We are treating BabyCheck as a Class IIa device and our CE marking under MDR is in progress, with vigilance reporting and a clinical advisory board that meets quarterly already set up. We are not fully CE-marked yet, so the conformity work is ongoing rather than complete.

app_description: BreathEasy is a Bluetooth-inhaler companion for paediatric asthma. Tracks rescue-inhaler usage, detects over-use, nudges children + parents to adhere to controller medication. EU. Children 6-16. Available in EN, DE, FR.
developer_persona: Pediatric-pulmonology PhD founder.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Inhaler use events (Bluetooth), peak flow when entered, adherence streaks, parent dashboard.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Parental consent + child assent (where age >= 12).
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class IIa under MDR.
simulated_answers.user_research: Co-designed with paediatric pulmonology clinics.
simulated_answers.accessibility: Kid-friendly UI in EN/DE/FR; parent dashboard standard.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Pilot study N=120 kids; 28% improved adherence.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Rule-based detection.
simulated_answers.post_market: Vigilance + monthly performance review.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: With prescribing pulmonologist on opt-in.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Parent or child (12+) can withdraw; family migration if change of carer.

expected_risks.risk: Children's data is special-category under GDPR; consent + assent + age verification all required.
Gamified adherence streaks may push kids to use inhaler when not needed.
Over-use detection threshold based on absolute count is age-naive; varies by season + activity.
If app alerts parent first about over-use, GP appointment may be delayed.
Older children's autonomy: 12-year-olds should be able to see their own data, not only via parents.
EN/DE/FR coverage misses IT, ES, PL etc.; paediatric idioms vary.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Age verification + parental consent flow + ICO/CNPD-compliant child consent; document data-protection impact assessment (DPIA).
Replace adherence 'streaks' with controller-medication 'plan completion' badges; avoid rescue-inhaler counters as positive metric.
Child-mode UI with age-appropriate view; explicit 'my data' section for ages 12+.
Personalized over-use threshold based on baseline + season; alert escalation to pulmonologist (not just parent).

notes: Paediatric scenario: child + parent consent + gamification + autonomy at 12+.

dev_facts.fact: Our entire user base is children aged 6-16, so we're handling special-category health data on minors; we collect parental consent plus child assent from age 12, but I'll admit we haven't built any real age-verification step beyond what the parent self-declares at sign-up.

We deliberately gamified adherence with streaks to keep kids engaged, but the streak mechanic rewards inhaler logging events, and I haven't fully thought through whether that could nudge a child to puff the rescue inhaler when they don't clinically need to.

Our over-use detection is rule-based and fires on an absolute count of rescue-inhaler events, and right now that threshold is the same for a six-year-old and a sixteen-year-old; it doesn't adjust for the child's age, the season, or how active they were that day.

When we detect over-use, the alert lands on the parent dashboard first, and we only escalate to the prescribing pulmonologist if the family has opted into data-sharing, so I recognize there's a real chance a needed clinician appointment gets delayed.

The app is built around the parent dashboard, and while a child of 12 or older can give assent and withdraw, we don't yet give those older kids a proper 'my data' view of their own inhaler usage independent of their parents.

We only ship in English, German and French, so we don't cover Italian, Spanish, Polish or other EU markets yet, and our kid-friendly copy was written and clinic-reviewed mainly for those three languages without separate validation of paediatric idioms elsewhere.

We're processing children's health data under MDR as a Class IIa device, but I have to admit we haven't formally appointed a DPO or completed a documented DPIA yet, even though I know one is clearly warranted given the population we serve.

app_description: PainTrack is a chronic-pain diary: daily intensity, body-map annotation, free-text triggers. Exports a PDF summary to the pain clinic. Available EU; integrates with FHIR-enabled EHRs where available.
developer_persona: Anaesthesiologist + dev co-founder duo.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Pain intensity (1-10), body map annotations, triggers (free text), medication taken, mood.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Standard onboarding consent + clinician integration toggle.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class I medical device.
simulated_answers.user_research: Beta-tested with 60 chronic-pain patients.
simulated_answers.accessibility: EN, DE, FR. WCAG basics.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Pain scale validated (NRS).
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI.
simulated_answers.post_market: Annual safety review.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Patient-controlled clinician sharing.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Data export + deletion.

expected_risks.risk: FHIR integration depends on EHR vendor maturity; partial integrations can confuse clinicians.
Daily logging fatigue; patients may stop or be inconsistent, undermining trend value.
Pain reporting is highly subjective; patient must control what is shared with clinician (e.g., recreational drug use should be redactable).
Free-text triggers can include sensitive info (illegal substances, abuse mentions); needs robust local encryption.
PDF summary aggregation methodology must be clear to clinician (mean vs median vs max).

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Profile to IHE PCC-7 or QRPH-58 (Patient Care Coordination); graceful degradation when FHIR endpoints missing.
Flexible reminder cadence; skip-without-penalty model; weekly recap that fills gaps.
User reviews/edits the PDF before clinician sees it.
Free-text encrypted with user-only key on device; cloud holds encrypted blobs only.

notes: Simple self-report scenario — eval whether the copilot pushes for FHIR interop, user data control, and acknowledges subjectivity of pain reporting.

dev_facts.fact: We integrate with FHIR-enabled EHRs where the clinic supports it, but the maturity varies a lot by vendor, so plenty of our clinics still just receive the exported PDF summary. When a clinic only has a partial FHIR endpoint, our handling for that case isn't really worked out yet.

PainTrack is a daily diary, so by design it nudges patients to log every day, and in our beta of 60 patients we already saw logging drop off over time. Right now an inconsistent week just shows up as gaps in the trend; the diary doesn't adapt its reminders to that.

Pain is subjective, so we're clear that this is a diary and the clinician makes the call, and the patient controls whether to share via the integration toggle. But the PDF generates from whatever they logged, including free-text things like recreational drug use, and once they've opted in the clinic sees that as-is.

Data sits both on-device and in our EU cloud, encrypted in transit and at rest. The free-text trigger field can capture sensitive stuff like substance use or abuse mentions, and I'll admit it's encrypted with our keys rather than a user-only on-device key, so technically we hold the plaintext capability.

The PDF summary shows pain trends over time, but I'll be honest, we don't spell out the aggregation method on the page, so a clinician can't immediately tell whether a number is a mean, median, or peak intensity.

Consent is a standard onboarding screen plus a separate toggle for clinician integration. We don't offer granular per-data-type consent yet — within the diary it's all-or-nothing, though the clinician sharing is at least a distinct opt-in.

The app ships in English, German, and French and we've covered WCAG basics like contrast and labels, but we haven't run a full WCAG 2.1 AA audit, and we haven't specifically tested the free-text and body-map flows with screen-reader users or for lower-literacy patients.

It's a standard smartphone app and the diary itself works offline; FHIR sync needs connectivity but the PDF route doesn't. We haven't thought through shared-device or low-data-plan situations, and we don't have a defined affordability or low-income access policy.

We've classified PainTrack as a Class I medical device under MDR 2017/745 and we're self-certifying on that basis, since Class I doesn't require a notified body. Our technical documentation exists but I wouldn't call it fully complete or audit-ready yet.

We process health data, so we rely on GDPR Art. 9 as our lawful basis, and patients can export and delete their data. We haven't formally appointed a DPO or completed a documented DPIA yet — that's still on our list.

app_description: InflamaTrack is a journal for IBD (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis) patients: stool frequency, urgency, bleeding, food triggers. Anonymized data is shared with a gastroenterology research consortium (opt-in). EU + CH.
developer_persona: Research-affiliated startup; sometimes blurs research/product lines.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Symptom logs (frequency, severity, bleeding), food triggers, medication adherence, mood, biometrics from wearable (optional).
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Two-layer: app usage + research consortium opt-in (with detailed PIS).
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class I; research arm IRB-approved.
simulated_answers.user_research: Co-designed with IBD patient association.
simulated_answers.accessibility: WCAG; DE/FR/IT/EN.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Symptom logging is observational; no claims.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI.
simulated_answers.post_market: Annual safety review.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Anonymized data to research consortium with explicit opt-in; aggregated reports to patients.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Withdraw from research at any time; future data not shared; published data remains as published.

expected_risks.risk: 'Anonymized' IBD data can be re-identified via symptom pattern + medication + geographic info; k-anonymity threshold must be set.
Right to withdraw must be granular: 'don't share my data with the consortium any more' AND 'delete previously shared data where possible'.
IBD symptoms (bleeding, stool) are highly intimate; data leak has stigmatizing potential.
Research-consortium partners: how many, who, where? List should be visible to user.
Audit log of who accessed user's data in the consortium must be available to user.
User must understand what 'opt in to research' actually means and how it differs from 'use the app'.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Use HE / synthetic data or k≥50 anonymization; audit by external statistician.
Dynamic consent dashboard; per-partner opt-out; clear language about what can/cannot be undone.
Live list of research partners + their purpose + how to contact them; updated within 24h.
Per-user access log: who, when, what data.

notes: Patient-research overlap; tests for re-identification risk, dynamic consent, and audit access.

dev_facts.fact: Honestly, our anonymization for the consortium feed is just stripping the obvious direct identifiers — name, email, device ID — before export; we haven't set a k-anonymity threshold or had a statistician audit it, so I'll concede that someone could probably re-link a record from a distinctive stool/bleeding pattern plus a specific medication and the EU/CH region. On the erasure side, in-app account deletion wipes our own copy, but I can't promise we can claw back rows already handed to the research consortium.

Right now withdrawal is all-or-nothing through a 'leave the research programme' toggle that stops any future data going to the consortium, and you keep full use of the journal either way — but we don't have a granular per-partner opt-out or a dynamic consent dashboard yet. Anything already shared and published stays as published; I tell people clearly that we can stop the flow but can't necessarily delete what's already out there.

We don't classify our users as a vulnerable population in our metadata — it's adult IBD patients — but I'm very aware stool frequency, urgency and rectal bleeding are about as intimate and stigmatizing as health data gets, so a leak would be genuinely damaging. Beyond our standard security and the participant information sheet, we haven't built any extra protections specifically tailored to how sensitive this category is.

The only third party we share with is the gastroenterology research consortium, and only for opt-in users — no analytics SDKs, no advertisers, no data brokers. That said, we don't currently surface a live, named list of the consortium member institutions or their contact details inside the app; the partners are described in general terms in the participant information sheet rather than itemized.

We keep internal records of our own exports to the consortium, but we don't expose a per-user access log showing which research institution accessed which of your records and when — a user can't pull up a 'who looked at my data' trail today. That's a gap I'd admit; the consortium's own internal access is largely opaque to us once the dataset is handed over.

We're explicit that InflamaTrack is an observational symptom journal — no diagnosis, no treatment recommendations, no claims — and the screens reinforce that it doesn't replace your gastroenterologist. Where I think the messaging is weakest is making the gap between 'using the app' and 'opting into research' unmistakable; some users probably don't fully register that the consortium opt-in is a separate, additional act on top of normal app usage.

Consent is genuinely two layers — basic app-usage terms, then a separate research-consortium opt-in backed by a detailed participant information sheet — and we co-designed the wording with an IBD patient association to keep it plain. Within a layer it's fairly coarse though: you opt into the research bundle as a whole rather than choosing, say, to share symptom logs but not your optional wearable biometrics.

We don't do any clinical interoperability today — no HL7 FHIR, no SNOMED CT, no read/write to hospital EHRs. Users can optionally pull in biometrics from a wearable, but there's no standards-based exchange with other health systems, and that isn't on our near-term roadmap.

It's a standard smartphone app, localized in DE/FR/IT/EN and built to WCAG, so we've tried to keep the access bar low across the EU and Switzerland. We haven't specifically designed for shared-device households or very low digital-literacy users, and the optional wearable integration does assume you own a compatible device — so that piece isn't equally available to everyone.

Our research arm is IRB-approved and we treat the data as GDPR Art. 9 special category, leaning on Art. 89 research provisions and Swiss HRA for the consortium side. I'll be candid that I'm not 100% sure we have a formally appointed DPO or a completed DPIA on file for the product itself — that's the kind of thing the research/product split sometimes blurs for us, and I'd have to check whether it's actually documented.

app_description: VoiceMind is a hospital-waiting-room kiosk that records a 60-second voice sample, runs an ML model that flags depression risk, and notifies the front desk to suggest an appointment. Designed for primary-care clinics. EU.
developer_persona: AI researcher founder, technically strong, regulation-fluent on paper.

simulated_answers.data_collected: 60-second audio, ML model output (risk score), front-desk action.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Patient signs consent on the kiosk before recording.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Class IIa SaMD under MDR; CE marking in progress.
simulated_answers.user_research: Tested with 5 primary-care clinics.
simulated_answers.accessibility: Voice-only is exclusionary for users with speech difficulties.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Validation N=400 patients vs PHQ-9; AUROC 0.82.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: Speech model (Wav2Vec) + classifier head.
simulated_answers.post_market: Quarterly performance review; vigilance reporting.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: Audio kept 7 days for incident review; embeddings retained 1 year.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Patient can request audio deletion.

expected_risks.risk: Consent in a waiting room is coercive; user can't easily refuse a kiosk in front of receptionist + queue.
Mental-health flagging in a public-ish space → social stigma + potential overheard front-desk discussion.
Voice models are sensitive to accent, language, age; AUROC 0.82 overall may hide much worse subgroup performance.
Front desk sees a risk score with no clinical context; may over-trigger appointments.
Front-desk staff are not clinicians; risk of automation bias driving inappropriate handling.
Voice-only excludes users with speech impairments, severe accent, language other than supported.
Audio retention 7 days in a kiosk environment — physical security?
Black-box risk score; clinician needs to know why this patient was flagged.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Private consent flow in a separate room; explicit 'No, thanks' option that is not visible to staff.
Subgroup evaluation by accent/age/sex; refuse to score outside validated language scope.
Front desk never sees raw score; only a 'consider asking the patient if they'd like to talk to someone' suggestion.
Alternative consent path: text-based PHQ-9 on the kiosk; user can choose.
Clinician dashboard shows top driving voice features (pitch variability, speech rate) with caveats.

expected_regulations_cited: EU AI Act Art. 5 (manipulative/exploitative if pressure)

notes: Stigma + consent-in-waiting-room + bias + automation bias by non-clinicians. Many high-stakes catches.

dev_facts.fact: I'll be honest that the consent flow is technically clean but contextually weak: the patient signs on the kiosk in the open waiting room, often with a receptionist and a queue right there. I haven't designed a genuinely private 'No, thanks' path, so the refusal option isn't something a patient can take without it being visible to staff and other people waiting.

The kiosk sits in a semi-public waiting room and the output is a depression-risk flag that lands at the front desk, so yes, there's a real stigma exposure — a non-clinical receptionist could end up discussing a mental-health flag where others might overhear. We haven't formalized how the front-desk handoff stays confidential in a shared space.

Our headline number is AUROC 0.82 on N=400 against PHQ-9, but I'll concede that's an aggregate and we haven't run subgroup evaluation by accent, age, sex, or dialect. Wav2Vec-based speech models are known to be sensitive to exactly those factors, so the overall number almost certainly hides worse performance for some groups, and we don't currently refuse to score voices outside our validated profile.

Right now the front desk effectively sees the model's risk output and a suggestion to offer an appointment, with no clinical context attached. I can see the over-triggering risk — a receptionist acting on a raw score with no nuance — and we haven't reduced what they see down to a neutral 'consider asking if they'd like to talk to someone' prompt.

The people receiving the flag are front-desk staff, not clinicians, and I'll admit that's a structural weak point: there's a real automation-bias risk that they treat the score as authoritative and handle the patient inappropriately. We haven't built clinician-in-the-loop gating before a flag reaches a non-clinical staffer.

I already accept that voice-only is exclusionary — anyone with a speech impairment, a heavy accent, or a language we don't support is effectively shut out or mis-scored. We don't currently offer an alternative path like a text-based PHQ-9 on the kiosk, so right now there's no equivalent route for those users.

We keep the 60-second audio for 7 days for incident review and embeddings for a year, but this lives on a kiosk in a clinic, and I'll be straight that I haven't pinned down the physical and at-rest security of that device — who can access it locally, whether the audio is encrypted on the box, and how it's protected if the kiosk is tampered with.

The classifier produces a risk score but it's essentially a black box to the end users — a clinician can't currently see why a given patient was flagged. We don't yet surface the driving voice features like pitch variability or speech rate, so there's no explanation a doctor could sanity-check the flag against.

Strictly, the only data we need for the function is the 60-second sample, the resulting risk score, and the front-desk action. I'd argue we're fairly lean, but retaining raw audio for 7 days and embeddings for a full year goes beyond the bare minimum needed to just produce and act on the score, and we haven't pressure-tested those retention windows against data minimization.

My legal basis is patient consent captured on the kiosk, and I treat this as GDPR Article 9 special-category health data. On paper that's the framing, but given the waiting-room setting I haven't fully stress-tested whether that consent is actually freely given, or whether we should be leaning on a clinical/health-provision basis instead.

It's a fixed kiosk capturing voice and pushing a flag to the front desk over the clinic network, and honestly I've focused more on the model than on the end-to-end system integrity — I haven't formalized how we protect against tampering, spoofed audio inputs, or the notification channel being intercepted between the kiosk and the desk.

Front-desk access to the flags and the retained embeddings is something we haven't locked down with formal role-based controls or audit logging. I can't yet tell you exactly who at a clinic can see historical scores or audio, or how we'd securely delete embeddings on a legal request — that access-governance layer isn't formalized.

We validated and operate within a limited language scope, and I'll admit we haven't separately validated performance across the different languages and dialects you'd actually hit across the EU. The kiosk doesn't currently detect when a speaker is out of our validated language scope and refuse to score, so cross-population robustness is unproven.

I'm clear on this one: we're treating VoiceMind as Class IIa SaMD under MDR Rule 11 because it's software informing a clinical decision, and CE marking is in progress. That classification work is the part I'm most confident about.

I'm regulation-fluent on the MDR side, but I'll concede I've done less concrete work on the EU AI Act. A depression-risk classifier for healthcare almost certainly lands in the Annex III high-risk bucket, and I haven't completed a formal AI Act classification or the conformity work that goes with it — I've been treating MDR as the primary lens.

Our post-market plan is a quarterly performance review plus MDR vigilance reporting, which exists on paper. What I haven't fully operationalized is the trigger and process for acting on a single dangerous output — say a clear false negative on a high-risk patient — beyond folding it into the periodic review.

app_description: ImpfPlan is a vaccination reminder for children. Parents enter the child's birth date; the app schedules reminders matching the Swiss BAG vaccination calendar. Available in DE/FR/IT (Swiss official languages) + EN. Free, no monetization.
developer_persona: Public-health-minded indie developer.

simulated_answers.data_collected: Child birth date, name (optional), parent email.
simulated_answers.consent_flow: Standard consent; parental responsibility checkbox.
simulated_answers.regulatory_status: Wellness; we don't make medical recommendations beyond the BAG calendar.
simulated_answers.user_research: Pilot with 50 families.
simulated_answers.accessibility: DE/FR/IT/EN; large fonts.
simulated_answers.safety_validation: Schedule mirrors BAG; we update when BAG updates.
simulated_answers.ai_or_algorithm: No AI.
simulated_answers.post_market: Annual BAG calendar refresh.
simulated_answers.data_sharing: None.
simulated_answers.withdrawal_rights: Account delete.

expected_risks.risk: If BAG updates the calendar (e.g., new vaccine, change of timing) and the app's data isn't refreshed promptly, missed vaccinations occur.
Children's data; consent flow for parental responsibility must be robust.
Offline use case (rural CH) — does the app need internet to compute the next reminder?
Vaccine hesitancy: app must clearly say 'this is a reminder, not a medical recommendation specific to your child'.
Could be Class I SaMD if interpreted as patient-specific medical advice; safer to mirror BAG exactly.
Email collection for free reminder; could use just local notifications.

expected_mitigations.mitigation: Subscribe to BAG calendar feed; flag stale data in UI; force update on launch if >30 days old.
Parental consent + capacity to opt-out child once age of consent reached (CH varies).
Pre-compute all reminders offline at install; sync only when calendar updates.
Onboarding screen: 'This is the official BAG calendar. Talk to your paediatrician about your child's specific situation.'

expected_regulations_cited: Swiss BAG/Bundesamt für Gesundheit vaccination calendar

notes: Simple Swiss-flavoured paediatric scenario; tests for staleness detection, offline robustness, and respect for parental autonomy + clinician primacy.

dev_facts.fact: Honestly, our update process is manual — once a year I copy the latest BAG calendar into the app, so if BAG changes a vaccine or timing mid-year a family could be working off a stale schedule until my next refresh.

I know I'm handling children's data, so entry is gated behind a parental-responsibility checkbox, but I'll admit I haven't built anything for the child to opt out or take over the account once they reach the Swiss age of consent.

I haven't actually verified the offline behaviour for rural users — I believe the reminders compute locally after setup, but I never formally tested that the app works with no connection, so I can't promise it.

We just mirror the official BAG calendar and never make recommendations specific to a child, but I have to confess we don't yet have an explicit screen telling parents to talk to their paediatrician — it's something I keep meaning to add.

I consider us wellness, not a medical device, precisely because we copy the BAG calendar verbatim and don't give patient-specific advice — I haven't sought any formal Swissmedic or regulatory classification.

We collect the parent's email mainly so I can send reminder notifications, plus the child's birth date and an optional name — I haven't really weighed whether local-only notifications would let me drop the email entirely.
I keep it deliberately minimal — child birth date, optional name, and parent email — because the app is free with no monetization, so there's no business reason for me to gather anything more.
Accessibility-wise I offer all four languages, DE, FR, IT and EN, and larger fonts, but beyond that I haven't done any formal accessibility audit like screen-reader or contrast testing.
My post-market plan is basically the annual BAG calendar refresh and I ran a small pilot with 50 families; I don't have a structured incident-reporting or adverse-event channel set up yet.
